items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In Figure 1, corticosteroids are shown blocking the pathway at the "Membrane Phospholipids → Arachidonic Acid" step, while NSAIDs act one step later. What does this positioning explain?

options.A: Corticosteroids act upstream of NSAIDs, which is why they can suppress a broader range of inflammatory mediators, not just prostaglandins
options.B: Corticosteroids and NSAIDs block the exact same enzyme
options.D: Neither drug class affects the arachidonic acid pathway

items.why: By inhibiting phospholipase A₂, corticosteroids block the release of arachidonic acid itself — upstream of COX — which is why they suppress a broader range of inflammatory mediators (not just prostaglandins) than NSAIDs, which act only at the COX step.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which mediator is the primary target of NSAID therapy within the inflammatory pain pathway?

options.D: Cytokines broadly (e.g., all of TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6)

items.why: NSAIDs inhibit COX enzymes, directly reducing prostaglandin synthesis. Histamine, bradykinin, and cytokines are important inflammatory mediators too, but they are not the primary target of NSAID mechanism.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In acetaminophen overdose, hepatotoxicity results primarily from which mechanism?

options.A: Direct COX inhibition in the liver
options.C: Accumulation of NAPQI after glutathione stores are depleted

items.why: NAPQI, normally detoxified by conjugation with glutathione, accumulates once glutathione stores are exhausted in overdose, causing hepatocyte injury — which is why N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) is the antidote.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Based on Figure 2, a patient with a history of GI ulcer but no cardiovascular disease is switched from ibuprofen to celecoxib. What is the most likely net effect on this patient’s risk profile?

options.A: Lower GI risk, with some increase in cardiovascular risk
options.B: Both GI and cardiovascular risk decrease
options.C: No change in either risk, since all NSAIDs carry identical risk profiles
options.D: Both GI and cardiovascular risk increase

items.why: Figure 2 shows celecoxib’s illustrative GI-risk bar is lower than the nonselective NSAID bar, while its cardiovascular-risk bar is higher — exactly the trade-off described in the celecoxib bullet slide. For this GI-ulcer-history patient without cardiovascular disease, that trade may be favorable, but the increased cardiovascular risk should still be discussed.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with CKD, hypertension, and anticoagulant use needs analgesia for osteoarthritis. Which class carries the highest combined renal and bleeding risk for this patient?
items.why: This patient has multiple NSAID red flags at once: CKD (renal risk), anticoagulant use (bleeding risk), and hypertension (cardiovascular risk) — oral NSAIDs carry the highest combined risk here.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In Figure 3, which biologic DMARD acts earliest in the cascade shown, before cytokines like TNF-α and IL-6 are even released?
items.why: Abatacept blocks T-cell costimulation — the step furthest upstream in the diagram, occurring before activated T cells drive cytokine release (blocked downstream by adalimumab/tocilizumab) or B-cell activity (blocked by rituximab).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which feature distinguishes a DMARD from an NSAID in the management of rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: DMARDs provide faster pain relief than NSAIDs
options.B: NSAIDs suppress the immune system more potently than DMARDs
options.C: DMARDs modify the underlying disease process rather than only masking symptoms
options.D: DMARDs are only available as biologic agents

items.why: An NSAID can make a patient feel better without changing RA’s disease trajectory; a DMARD (conventional or biologic) is intended to slow or halt joint destruction and systemic inflammation itself.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In acetaminophen overdose, why is N-acetylcysteine effective?

options.A: It speeds renal excretion of unchanged acetaminophen
options.B: It is a glutathione precursor that restores NAPQI detoxification
options.C: It blocks COX in the liver and lowers prostaglandin levels
options.D: It inhibits the enzyme that forms NAPQI from the drug
options.E: It binds acetaminophen in the gut and prevents absorption

items.why: Overdose depletes glutathione so NAPQI accumulates; N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI (S19; SG U2-R3).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 40-year-old with an acutely swollen, inflamed knee asks for the drug that best treats the inflammation itself. Why is acetaminophen not the best choice?

options.A: It only works when given intravenously in hospital
options.B: It causes more GI bleeding than the NSAIDs do
options.C: It is contraindicated in anyone with joint swelling
options.D: Its anti-inflammatory effect at the periphery is minimal
options.E: It has no analgesic effect in musculoskeletal pain

items.why: Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever centrally, but its peripheral anti-inflammatory effect is minimal — it is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent (S15).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which statement best explains why nonselective NSAIDs cause GI and renal adverse effects?

options.A: They block TNF-α, which normally protects the stomach lining
options.B: They block phospholipase A₂ and stop all mediator release
options.C: They inhibit COX-1, which protects gastric mucosa and renal blood flow
options.D: They inhibit COX-2, the only source of protective prostaglandins
options.E: They deplete glutathione, which injures the gut and kidney

items.why: COX-1 is the housekeeping enzyme that maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it contributes to GI and renal adverse effects (S26; SG U2-R4).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) and hydrochlorothiazide starts daily naproxen for knee pain. Two weeks later, creatinine has risen sharply. What pattern explains this?

options.A: Expected COX-2 renal protection failing under stress
options.B: Bleeding from the NSAID plus the ACE inhibitor together
options.C: The “triple whammy”: NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic causing AKI
options.D: A GI ulcer from NSAID plus diuretic, causing dehydration
options.E: Hepatotoxicity from NAPQI formed by naproxen metabolism

items.why: NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors/ARBs raise AKI risk, and adding a diuretic is the high-yield “triple whammy” AKI pattern (S36; S36 notes).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which nonselective NSAID does the lecture restrict to short-term use because of significant GI and renal risk?
items.why: Ketorolac is for short-term use only because of significant GI/renal risk (S28).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient takes low-dose aspirin for cardioprotection and starts regular ibuprofen for back pain. What is the textbook concern?

options.A: Ibuprofen converts aspirin to the toxic metabolite NAPQI
options.B: Ibuprofen speeds aspirin’s renal excretion fivefold
options.C: Ibuprofen blocks aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition
options.D: Aspirin makes ibuprofen COX-2 selective, raising CV risk
options.E: Both drugs together protect the kidney from injury

items.why: Concomitant ibuprofen antagonizes aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition, limiting its cardioprotective effect (p. 680).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 66-year-old has knee pain worse with activity, no systemic symptoms, and mild disease. Which first-line drug does the lecture call reasonable?
items.why: Acetaminophen is a reasonable first-line for mild OA pain (S43).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: What is the key difference in treatment goals between osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: Both aim only at pain relief with NSAIDs
options.B: OA aims at cartilage regrowth with DMARDs
options.C: OA aims at pain and function; RA aims to suppress disease activity
options.D: OA aims to suppress immunity; RA aims at pain relief only
options.E: RA aims at weight loss; OA aims at infection control

items.why: OA treatment targets pain control and function; RA treatment must suppress disease activity, not just pain (S41).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient newly started on methotrexate for RA asks whether to take a tablet every morning “to keep levels steady.” What is the correct counseling?

options.A: Take it daily but skip the folate supplement
options.B: Take it only on days when joints are painful
options.C: Take it twice daily, like naproxen, for steady levels
options.D: Take it once weekly, because daily dosing can be fatal
options.E: Take it daily with food to reduce stomach upset

items.why: Methotrexate is dosed weekly, not daily — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal (S49; SG U2-R7).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: What is methotrexate’s mechanism as taught in the lecture, and what is co-prescribed to reduce its toxicity?

options.A: COX-2 inhibition; a proton pump inhibitor

items.why: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses; folate is routinely co-prescribed (S49; SG U2-R7; SG U2-M).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 29-year-old with active RA who is planning a pregnancy needs a DMARD. Which drug from the lecture is contraindicated?

options.A: Celecoxib, because it is a disease-modifying drug
options.B: Sulfasalazine, because it is only used alone
options.C: Acetaminophen, because it is a DMARD
options.E: Hydroxychloroquine, because of its poor safety profile

items.why: Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy because it is teratogenic (S49).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Before starting adalimumab for rheumatoid arthritis, which baseline step does the lecture specifically call for?

options.A: Screening for tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C
options.B: Starting folate to prevent bone marrow toxicity
options.C: Adding an ACE inhibitor to protect the kidney
options.D: Checking for all hidden acetaminophen sources
options.E: Avoiding all vaccines until therapy has begun

items.why: Biologics cause immunosuppression; baseline tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C screening comes before starting them (S56).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on a biologic DMARD calls with a fever of 38.6 °C and a productive cough. What lecture principle drives the advice to be seen promptly?

options.A: NSAID-like renal toxicity makes fever dangerous
options.B: Fever means the biologic is working as intended
options.C: Immunosuppression raises infection risk across all DMARDs
options.D: Biologics raise cardiovascular risk like celecoxib

items.why: The major safety theme across all DMARDs is immunosuppression → increased infection risk; patients should report fevers or infection symptoms promptly (S56; SG U2-R8).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Match the drug to its target: which pairing is correct?
items.why: Tocilizumab is the lecture’s IL-6 inhibitor (S51; SG U2-R8).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with RA and high cardiovascular risk is being considered for tofacitinib. Which boxed warning applies to all JAK inhibitors?

options.A: Lymphoma only, exactly the same as the TNF inhibitors
options.B: Teratogenicity that requires strict weekly-only dosing
options.C: Retinopathy that requires annual eye examinations
options.D: Venous thromboembolism, major cardiovascular events, and cancer
options.E: Fatal hepatotoxicity from NAPQI accumulating in the liver

items.why: All JAK inhibitors carry an FDA boxed warning for VTE (DVT, PE), MACE, and cancer (p. 686).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which conventional DMARD requires a baseline eye exam and annual screening after 5 years because of retinopathy?
items.why: Antimalarials bind melanin-rich tissue such as the retina; a baseline exam and annual screening after 5 years are recommended (p. 684).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient using acetaminophen for back pain also takes a nighttime sleep aid and a cold-and-flu product. What should the PA do first?

options.A: Review every product label for hidden acetaminophen
options.B: Reassure that OTC products are always safe
options.D: Check a creatinine for NSAID renal injury
options.E: Switch the back-pain drug to celecoxib at once

items.why: Many combination cold, flu, and sleep products contain acetaminophen; unintentional double-dosing is a leading cause of acetaminophen liver injury, so ask about all sources.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which non-drug approaches does the lecture include in osteoarthritis management?
items.why: OA management includes activity modification, physical therapy, and weight management alongside drugs.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A runner sprained an ankle yesterday; the pain is sharp and clearly tied to the injury. How is this pain best classified by time course?
items.why: Acute pain has recent onset and is often tied to an identifiable injury or flare.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient from a region with high tuberculosis rates is about to start adalimumab. Which step matters most before the first dose?

options.D: Screen for TB and hepatitis B/C

items.why: Immunosuppression is the shared DMARD risk; baseline TB and hepatitis B/C screening comes before biologics (TNF inhibitors can reactivate TB and hepatitis B).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient stable on warfarin is started on celecoxib for osteoarthritis. What should the clinician anticipate?

options.C: No change, since celecoxib spares platelets
options.E: Higher bleeding risk — monitor INR closely

items.why: NSAIDs plus anticoagulants raise bleeding risk; the textbook adds that celecoxib (a CYP2C9 substrate) occasionally interacts with warfarin.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which set lists methotrexate's key adverse effects from the lecture?
items.why: Methotrexate's key adverse effects are hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, and pulmonary toxicity; folate reduces toxicity.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient takes 4 g of acetaminophen daily plus a nightly cold-and-flu product, and drinks alcohol heavily. Three weeks later, AST and ALT are markedly elevated. What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.B: Stop all acetaminophen and work up liver injury
options.C: Double the acetaminophen dose to control the pain
options.D: Continue and repeat liver tests in six months
options.E: Ignore it — acetaminophen is safe at any dose

items.why: Hidden acetaminophen in combination products plus chronic alcohol use (↓ glutathione, ↑ CYP2E1) raises NAPQI injury risk; stop the suspected drug and work up liver injury.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.src: L03 S41; S41 (notes); S45 (notes); p. 676; p. 701
items.stem: A 45-year-old has symmetric hand-joint swelling, morning stiffness, and a positive rheumatoid factor. Why are NSAIDs alone not enough?

options.A: RA pain is neuropathic and needs nerve blockers
options.B: RA is degenerative, so only steroid injections work
options.C: NSAIDs have no analgesic effect in any arthritis
options.D: NSAIDs are contraindicated in everyone with RA
options.E: RA needs disease-modifying therapy, not pain relief alone

items.why: RA is an autoimmune, systemic inflammatory disease whose goal is to suppress disease activity; NSAIDs ease symptoms without altering the disease course.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: What defines a drug as “disease-modifying” in rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: It selectively blocks the COX-2 isoform
options.B: It slows or halts joint destruction
options.C: It lowers fever through the hypothalamus
options.D: It is given only as an injection
options.E: It relieves pain faster than NSAIDs

items.why: A DMARD is intended to alter the course of RA — slowing or halting joint destruction and systemic inflammation — rather than only masking symptoms.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which drug is a TNF inhibitor?
items.why: Adalimumab, etanercept, and infliximab are the lecture's TNF inhibitors.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient taking lisinopril and furosemide develops an acute gout flare. Which plan avoids the most predictable kidney injury?

options.A: Probenecid to flush uric acid through the kidney
options.B: Start allopurinol today to shorten the flare
options.D: Avoid an NSAID; treat with a short corticosteroid course
options.E: Celecoxib, because COX-2 selectivity spares the kidney

items.why: NSAID + ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic is the high-yield ‘triple whammy’ AKI pattern; a short corticosteroid course is a good flare alternative when NSAIDs are contraindicated.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient develops a GI bleed while taking a standard dose of naproxen. How is this adverse effect best classified?

options.A: Toxicity from an overdose above the range
options.D: Type A — predictable from COX-1 inhibition

items.why: Blocking COX-1 removes gastric mucosal protection and platelet TXA2 — GI bleeding is a predictable, dose-related extension of the drug’s action (Type A).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Per the textbook, which instruction about ketorolac is correct?

options.A: Double the dose in patients over 65
options.D: Start therapy with an oral dose

items.why: Ketorolac is for short-term use only (slides); the textbook adds a 120 mg/day maximum, halved doses in older, light, or renally impaired patients, and no more than 5 days.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 72-year-old with CKD, hypertension, and anticoagulation has an acute gout flare. Which option is often preferred?
items.why: With these risk factors an oral NSAID is relatively contraindicated; a short corticosteroid course (oral or intra-articular) is often preferred.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient taking lisinopril and furosemide develops an acute gout flare. Which plan avoids the most predictable kidney injury?

options.A: Avoid an NSAID; treat with a short corticosteroid course
options.B: Start allopurinol today to shorten the flare
options.C: Probenecid to flush uric acid through the kidney
options.E: Celecoxib, because COX-2 selectivity spares the kidney

items.why: NSAID + ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic is the high-yield ‘triple whammy’ AKI pattern; a short corticosteroid course is a good flare alternative when NSAIDs are contraindicated.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which statement correctly describes COX-1?

options.A: Enzyme that converts acetaminophen to NAPQI
options.B: Housekeeping enzyme protecting stomach and renal flow
options.D: Inducible enzyme found mainly at inflamed sites

items.why: COX-1 is the housekeeping enzyme that maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it contributes to GI and renal adverse effects.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman in her third trimester asks whether she can take naproxen for back pain. Based on the lecture, what is the best response?

options.A: Use ketorolac daily as a long-term option
options.B: Use it freely — NSAIDs are safest in late pregnancy
options.C: Use celecoxib instead — COX-2 drugs are exempt
options.D: Add folate to make naproxen safe
options.E: Avoid it — late pregnancy is an NSAID caution

items.why: The lecture lists late pregnancy among the conditions to use NSAIDs with caution or avoid.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with RA on adalimumab has a family history of lymphoma and asks about cancer risk. Which statement matches the textbook?

options.A: Boxed warnings apply only to IV biologics
options.B: Only methotrexate carries a malignancy warning
options.C: TNF inhibitors carry a boxed malignancy warning
options.D: Cancer risk applies only to JAK inhibitors
options.E: TNF inhibitors lower lymphoma risk to zero

items.why: The FDA placed a boxed warning on all anti-TNF agents about possible malignancy, especially lymphoma; periodic skin exams are advised.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 19-year-old arrives 4 hours after taking a large acetaminophen overdose. Which drug restores the pathway that detoxifies the toxic metabolite?
items.why: Overdose depletes glutathione, so NAPQI accumulates; N-acetylcysteine is a glutathione precursor that replenishes it to detoxify NAPQI.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient will start infliximab next month and is due for a live vaccine. When should the vaccine be given?

options.A: One week after the first infusion
options.C: Any time, since biologics don't affect immunity
options.D: Only if a fever develops on therapy
options.E: Never — vaccines are banned for life

items.why: Update vaccines — especially live vaccines — before starting DMARD therapy, because these drugs suppress the immune response.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: What defines a drug as “disease-modifying” in rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: It selectively blocks the COX-2 isoform
options.B: It relieves pain faster than NSAIDs
options.C: It lowers fever through the hypothalamus
options.D: It is given only as an injection
options.E: It slows or halts joint destruction

items.why: A DMARD is intended to alter the course of RA — slowing or halting joint destruction and systemic inflammation — rather than only masking symptoms.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Before starting adalimumab, a patient’s interferon-gamma release assay is positive. What is the most appropriate decision?

options.A: Give a live vaccine first to boost immunity
options.B: Treat latent TB before starting the TNF inhibitor
options.E: Start adalimumab now; TB screening is a formality

items.why: All DMARDs share infection risk; screen for TB and hepatitis B/C and update vaccines before starting a biologic, treating positives first.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with chronic alcohol use who has barely eaten for days takes acetaminophen at the upper end of normal dosing. Why is their liver risk higher?

options.A: Alcohol converts acetaminophen into an NSAID
options.B: Fasting saturates TXA2, causing hepatic bleeding
options.C: Lower glutathione plus induced CYP2E1 makes more NAPQI
options.D: Fasting speeds renal excretion of the parent drug
options.E: Alcohol blocks COX in the liver, adding NSAID toxicity

items.why: Chronic alcohol use and fasting lower glutathione (GSH) and both induce CYP2E1, so more drug becomes NAPQI and less can be neutralized.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A pharmacist calls: a new prescription reads “methotrexate 15 mg by mouth daily” for RA. What is the safety problem?

options.A: It should be IV only in RA
options.B: It needs N-acetylcysteine with each dose
options.C: It should be weekly; daily dosing can be fatal
options.D: It should be twice daily for steady levels
options.E: Nothing — daily dosing is standard for RA

items.why: Methotrexate is dosed weekly, not daily — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient stable on warfarin is started on celecoxib for osteoarthritis. What should the clinician anticipate?

options.B: No change, since celecoxib spares platelets
options.E: Higher bleeding risk — monitor INR closely

items.why: NSAIDs plus anticoagulants raise bleeding risk; the textbook adds that celecoxib (a CYP2C9 substrate) occasionally interacts with warfarin.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 22-year-old took a single large acetaminophen ingestion at a known time; a level drawn 8 hours later is 120 mcg/mL. Using the lecture's nomogram, what is the next step?

options.A: Discharge: levels fall below 150 by 8 hours
options.B: Ignore the level and treat with an NSAID
options.C: Wait until 24 hours for a second level first
options.D: Repeat the level before 4 hours have passed
options.E: Start NAC: the level is above the treatment line

items.why: On the Rumack-Matthew nomogram the slide's example — 8 h, 120 mcg/mL — is above the treatment line, so NAC is started (give early for best effect).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which sequence describes joint destruction in rheumatoid arthritis, as opposed to osteoarthritis?

options.A: Uric acid crystals deposit and trigger a flare
options.B: Synovitis forms a pannus; TNF-α and IL-6 drive erosion
options.C: Mechanical wear degrades cartilage; osteophytes form
options.D: NAPQI binds proteins in the synovial lining
options.E: Prostaglandin loss thins the gastric mucosa

items.why: RA is autoimmune: immune activation causes synovitis with pannus formation that erodes cartilage and bone, with TNF-α and IL-6 driving inflammation and damage — the cytokines biologics target.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A pharmacy label reads ‘methotrexate 15 mg by mouth daily’ for a new RA patient. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Dispense it — daily dosing gives faster control
options.B: Switch to IV methotrexate to bypass first-pass
options.C: Dispense it but halve the dose
options.D: Hold it; correct to once weekly with folate
options.E: Add an NSAID to protect the liver from toxicity

items.why: Methotrexate for RA is weekly only — daily dosing has caused fatal toxicity — with folate co-prescribed.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why is celecoxib associated with more cardiovascular events than its GI profile would suggest?

options.A: It depletes glutathione in the heart
options.B: It raises renal blood flow excessively
options.C: TXA2 falls while PGI2 is preserved
options.D: PGI2 falls while platelet TXA2 is preserved
options.E: It blocks COX-1 more than COX-2

items.why: Celecoxib blocks COX-2, lowering prostacyclin (PGI2) without a matching drop in platelet thromboxane (TXA2, made by spared COX-1) — the balance tips toward clotting.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient takes 4 g of acetaminophen daily plus a nightly cold-and-flu product, and drinks alcohol heavily. Three weeks later, AST and ALT are markedly elevated. What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.A: Continue and repeat liver tests in six months
options.B: Stop all acetaminophen and work up liver injury
options.D: Double the acetaminophen dose to control the pain
options.E: Ignore it — acetaminophen is safe at any dose

items.why: Hidden acetaminophen in combination products plus chronic alcohol use (↓ glutathione, ↑ CYP2E1) raises NAPQI injury risk; stop the suspected drug and work up liver injury.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with heart failure on furosemide develops worsening edema after starting high-dose ibuprofen. What best explains this?

options.A: Ibuprofen is a CYP inducer lowering furosemide
options.B: The edema is NAPQI-induced liver failure
options.C: Ibuprofen is COX-2 selective and hurts the heart
options.D: NSAIDs cause fluid retention and blunt diuretics

items.why: NSAIDs cause renal fluid retention and, with diuretics, reduce the diuretic effect and raise renal risk; heart failure is a caution for NSAID use.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 58-year-old with a prior bleeding ulcer and a recent myocardial infarction needs an anti-inflammatory. Why is celecoxib not a simple solution?

options.A: It raises GI risk but lowers cardiovascular risk
options.B: It has no effect on inflammatory prostaglandins
options.C: It lowers GI risk but raises cardiovascular risk
options.D: It is an antidote, not an anti-inflammatory
options.E: It protects the kidney but harms the liver

items.why: COX-2 selectivity gives a lower ulcer/bleeding risk but is associated with more cardiovascular events; renal risk is unchanged.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which non-drug approaches does the lecture include in osteoarthritis management?
items.why: OA management includes activity modification, physical therapy, and weight management alongside drugs.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with RA cannot tolerate methotrexate. Which conventional DMARD does the lecture name as the alternative?
items.why: Leflunomide is the alternative when methotrexate is not tolerated.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which sequence describes how tissue injury produces musculoskeletal pain?

options.A: Injury → glutathione loss → NAPQI build-up → pain
options.B: Injury → COX-1 induction → gastric protection → pain
options.C: Injury → nerve transection → cortical atrophy → pain
options.D: Injury → mediator release → nociceptor sensitization → pain
options.E: Injury → T-cell depletion → B-cell surge → pain

items.why: Tissue injury releases inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, cytokines) that sensitize nociceptors, producing pain.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A prescription reads infliximab. What does the stem “-ximab” tell you?
items.why: -ximab marks a chimeric antibody; infliximab is a chimeric anti-TNF-α antibody.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which effect is acetaminophen least reliable for?

options.A: Pain in a patient with CKD

items.why: Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever centrally, but its peripheral anti-inflammatory effect is minimal.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Three weeks after starting methotrexate for RA, a patient wants to stop it because the joints still ache. What is the best response?

options.A: Switch to daily dosing to speed the response
options.B: Continue: DMARD protection builds over weeks to months
options.C: Stop it — a DMARD that works relieves pain within days
options.D: Replace it with an NSAID to change the disease course
options.E: Add acetaminophen instead, since RA is degenerative

items.why: NSAIDs relieve symptoms in days, while DMARDs protect joints over weeks to months; DMARDs modify the disease course rather than just masking symptoms.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which drug is a TNF inhibitor?
items.why: Adalimumab, etanercept, and infliximab are the lecture's TNF inhibitors.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which drug pairing does the lecture flag for a higher GI ulcer risk?
items.why: NSAIDs combined with corticosteroids raise GI ulcer risk.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which NSAID is noted for oral and topical formulations?
items.why: Diclofenac is available in oral and topical formulations; topical NSAIDs give local relief with much lower systemic exposure.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient using acetaminophen for back pain also takes a nighttime sleep aid and a cold-and-flu product. What should the PA do first?

options.A: Review every product label for hidden acetaminophen
options.B: Switch the back-pain drug to celecoxib at once
options.C: Reassure that OTC products are always safe
options.D: Check a creatinine for NSAID renal injury

items.why: Many combination cold, flu, and sleep products contain acetaminophen; unintentional double-dosing is a leading cause of acetaminophen liver injury, so ask about all sources.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Rituximab treats rheumatoid arthritis by which mechanism?
items.why: Rituximab is B-cell targeted therapy: it depletes or modulates B lymphocytes.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which set lists methotrexate's key adverse effects from the lecture?
items.why: Methotrexate's key adverse effects are hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, and pulmonary toxicity; folate reduces toxicity.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.src: L03 S41; S41 (notes); S45 (notes); p. 676; p. 701
items.stem: A 45-year-old has symmetric hand-joint swelling, morning stiffness, and a positive rheumatoid factor. Why are NSAIDs alone not enough?

options.A: RA pain is neuropathic and needs nerve blockers
options.B: RA is degenerative, so only steroid injections work
options.C: NSAIDs have no analgesic effect in any arthritis
options.D: RA needs disease-modifying therapy, not pain relief alone
options.E: NSAIDs are contraindicated in everyone with RA

items.why: RA is an autoimmune, systemic inflammatory disease whose goal is to suppress disease activity; NSAIDs ease symptoms without altering the disease course.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why do corticosteroids suppress a broader range of inflammatory mediators than NSAIDs?

options.A: They neutralize TNF-α outside the cell
options.B: They deplete B cells that release prostaglandins
options.C: They block phospholipase A₂, upstream of COX
options.D: They block COX-2 more strongly than any NSAID
options.E: They act centrally on the hypothalamus

items.why: Corticosteroids block phospholipase A₂, preventing arachidonic acid release, so a broad range of mediators falls; NSAIDs act only at COX.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient from a region with high tuberculosis rates is about to start adalimumab. Which step matters most before the first dose?

options.E: Screen for TB and hepatitis B/C

items.why: Immunosuppression is the shared DMARD risk; baseline TB and hepatitis B/C screening comes before biologics (TNF inhibitors can reactivate TB and hepatitis B).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A runner sprained an ankle yesterday; the pain is sharp and clearly tied to the injury. How is this pain best classified by time course?
items.why: Acute pain has recent onset and is often tied to an identifiable injury or flare.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 70-year-old with knee OA has a flare limited to one knee despite acetaminophen and topical diclofenac. Which option does the lecture list for short-term relief?
items.why: Intra-articular corticosteroid injections give short-term relief for flares in a single joint.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on etanercept and methotrexate calls with a temperature of 38.6 °C and a productive cough, and wants a live vaccine before a trip next month. What is the best advice?

options.B: Continue etanercept; give the live vaccine now
options.E: Hold it, get seen now, skip the live vaccine

items.why: Immunosuppression raises infection risk: fever is infection until proven otherwise. Live vaccines are avoided on biologic or immunosuppressive therapy; update vaccines before starting. Abatacept is never combined with TNF inhibitors.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 63-year-old with knee osteoarthritis had a bleeding gastric ulcer last year and a sulfonamide allergy. Acetaminophen alone is not enough. Which option best fits?

options.B: Topical diclofenac gel on the knee
options.E: Ketorolac 10 mg every 6 hours for a month

items.why: Topical NSAIDs give local relief with much lower systemic exposure — a fit for knee OA when oral NSAIDs are risky. Celecoxib would spare the stomach but is contraindicated with sulfonamide allergy.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient's daughter calls: her mother has been taking her 'weekly' methotrexate 15 mg every morning for 6 days and now has mouth sores and a low white count. Which response is correct?

options.B: Hold one week, then resume the same daily dosing
options.C: Leucovorin rescue plus CBC, liver, kidney labs
options.D: Give extra folic acid and continue daily
options.E: Switch to a TNF inhibitor the same day

items.why: Methotrexate is 7.5–25 mg ONCE WEEKLY with folic acid 1 mg daily. Daily dosing by mistake causes severe toxicity (mucositis, myelosuppression); leucovorin is the rescue, with CBC, liver and creatinine monitoring.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 55-year-old who drinks 4–5 beers nightly has knee osteoarthritis and stage 3 CKD. He takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. Which analgesic plan fits best?

options.C: Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with food
options.D: Naproxen 500 mg twice daily for 2 weeks
options.E: Celecoxib 200 mg daily to spare the stomach

items.why: With CKD and an anticoagulant, NSAIDs carry the highest combined renal and bleeding risk, so acetaminophen is the safer first-line choice — but chronic alcohol use (or liver disease) lowers its maximum from 3–4 g/day to 2–3 g/day.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with RA and recurrent diverticulitis is being considered for tocilizumab. Which concern and monitoring plan fit?

options.A: GI perforation; monitor CBC, LFTs, lipids
options.B: Retinal toxicity; baseline and annual eye exams

items.why: Tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist): infection, elevated liver enzymes, neutropenia, hyperlipidemia and rare GI perforation — caution with diverticulitis; monitor CBC, liver enzymes and lipids.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 29-year-old man with RA on sulfasalazine says his urine is orange and he and his partner have not conceived. Which interpretation is right?

options.B: Infertility is permanent; stop all DMARDs
options.C: Orange urine signals hepatotoxicity, so stop it today
options.D: Expected sulfasalazine effects; sperm count recovers

items.why: Sulfasalazine adverse effects include orange urine and reversible oligospermia, plus nausea, rash, myelosuppression and hepatotoxicity (monitor CBC and liver tests).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Three days after coronary artery bypass grafting, a patient asks for something stronger than acetaminophen. Which statement about NSAIDs is correct here?

options.A: Celecoxib is safe because it spares COX-1
options.B: Ketorolac is preferred for up to 5 days
options.C: All are contraindicated in this setting
options.D: Ibuprofen is fine at OTC doses
options.E: Any NSAID is fine with a PPI added

items.why: The drug profiles list the CABG setting as a contraindication for ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, ketorolac (perioperative CABG) and celecoxib.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 24-year-old arrives 10 hours after taking a large amount of acetaminophen at once. The lab says a level will take 3 hours. What is the best next step?

options.A: Start NAC now; don't wait for the level
options.B: Give NAC only if symptoms of liver failure appear
options.C: Wait for the level, then plot it on the nomogram
options.D: Give activated charcoal only and observe
options.E: Plot a level only if AST and ALT are high

items.why: NAC replenishes glutathione and works best early, ideally within 8 hours. When presentation is late or a level is unavailable and the ingestion is significant, start NAC without waiting.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 68-year-old is given ketorolac after an orthopedic procedure. Which plan follows the drug profile?

options.A: Use it to bridge until celecoxib starts working
options.B: Switch to oral after 5 days for 2 more weeks
options.C: Standard dose, since age doesn't matter
options.D: Reduced dose for age, and 5 days or less in total
options.E: 30 mg IV every 6 hours for 10 days

items.why: Ketorolac is for short-term moderately severe acute pain: total course 5 days or less (max 120 mg/day IV/IM), reduced dose at age 65+, with boxed warnings for GI bleeding, renal failure, bleeding and CV events.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 50-kg woman with mild RA takes hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily and has a borderline-long QT on citalopram. Which change best follows the drug profile?

options.A: Stop eye exams since the dose is standard
options.B: Lower the dose to stay within 5 mg/kg/day
options.C: Raise to 600 mg for better RA control
options.D: Keep 400 mg; the maximum is per ideal weight
options.E: Add azithromycin to cover infection risk

items.why: Hydroxychloroquine: 200–400 mg daily, maximum 5 mg/kg/day actual body weight (here 250 mg). Retinal toxicity needs baseline and annual eye exams; caution with QT-prolonging drugs.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with RA who failed a TNF inhibitor is starting rituximab. Screening shows chronic hepatitis B. What should the clinician anticipate?

options.A: Faster RA response because of the infection
options.B: Only an infusion reaction, prevented by premedication
options.C: Risk of hepatitis B reactivation, a boxed warning
options.D: Lymphoma as the main risk at first infusion
options.E: No issue, since rituximab targets B cells only

items.why: Rituximab (anti-CD20) boxed warnings: infusion reactions, hepatitis B reactivation and PML. Screen hepatitis B first; premedicate with acetaminophen, an antihistamine and a steroid.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 46-year-old with RA not controlled on methotrexate has multiple sclerosis and NYHA class III heart failure. Which biologic choice is least appropriate?
items.why: TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, infliximab) are contraindicated with demyelinating disease and NYHA III–IV heart failure, besides active infection and untreated latent TB.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 70-year-old on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide, and lithium for bipolar disorder, starts daily naproxen for hip pain. Two weeks later he is confused and tremulous and his creatinine has risen. What best explains this?
items.why: NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic is the ‘triple whammy’ for AKI, and NSAIDs raise lithium levels — the falling kidney function drives lithium toxicity (confusion, tremor).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 31-year-old with RA has taken leflunomide for 2 years. She wants to become pregnant within the year. What is the most appropriate plan?

options.B: Continue it; it is safe in pregnancy
options.E: Stop it the week she conceives

items.why: Leflunomide (DHODH inhibitor) carries boxed warnings for hepatotoxicity and embryo-fetal toxicity; cholestyramine washout removes it. Methotrexate is also contraindicated in pregnancy.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why is dantrolene the malignant hyperthermia drug? MH is runaway calcium release through RyR1 in muscle; a CNS drug can’t reach that — dantrolene blocks RyR1 itself.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why does stopping intrathecal baclofen go badly? The spinal cord loses its GABA-B brake all at once: seizures, hyperthermia, and rebound spasticity.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why does stopping denosumab cause fractures? It blocks osteoclast formation without killing them; stop it and resorption rebounds — so hand off to a bisphosphonate.

items.text: Why the strict bisphosphonate rules? Under 1% is absorbed, and a tablet lodged in the esophagus burns it — fasting, plain water, upright.
