items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In Figure 4, probenecid and allopurinol both lower serum uric acid, but through different mechanisms. What is the key difference?

options.A: Probenecid increases renal excretion of uric acid; allopurinol decreases uric acid production
options.C: Probenecid decreases uric acid production; allopurinol increases renal excretion
options.D: Neither drug affects serum uric acid levels

items.why: Figure 4 shows allopurinol (and febuxostat) acting as xanthine oxidase inhibitors that reduce uric acid production, while probenecid acts at the kidney to increase renal excretion of uric acid that has already been produced — two different strategies for the same goal of lowering serum uric acid.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient presents with an acute gout flare. Which action is most appropriate at this visit?

options.A: Treat the acute flare (colchicine, NSAID, or corticosteroid) and defer urate-lowering therapy
options.B: Start allopurinol immediately to lower uric acid
options.D: No treatment is needed until uric acid is measured

items.why: Starting or changing urate-lowering therapy during an acute flare can worsen or prolong it. Treat the flare first; urate-lowering therapy is started or adjusted only once it resolves.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In Figure 5, which agent is the odd one out, acting directly on the skeletal muscle fiber rather than within the central nervous system?
items.why: Dantrolene decreases calcium release from the skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum, acting directly on the muscle fiber — unlike cyclobenzaprine, tizanidine, and baclofen, which all act within the CNS to reduce excitatory output to motor neurons.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which skeletal muscle relaxant acts directly on skeletal muscle itself (not the CNS), making it the agent of choice in malignant hyperthermia?
items.why: Dantrolene’s peripheral mechanism — decreasing calcium release from the skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum — is unique among these agents and is exactly why it is the emergency treatment for malignant hyperthermia.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In Figure 6, PTH release raises serum calcium through three parallel actions. Which organ system is NOT one of the three direct targets of PTH shown in the diagram?
items.why: PTH acts directly on bone (↑ osteoclast resorption) and kidney (↑ calcium reabsorption, activates vitamin D); its effect on the intestine is indirect, mediated through activated vitamin D. The lung is not part of this feedback loop at all.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Based on Figure 7, which bisphosphonate requires the fewest doses per year, and by what route is it given?

options.C: All bisphosphonates require the same number of annual doses

items.why: Figure 7 shows zoledronic acid dosed as infrequently as once yearly by IV infusion, versus weekly oral dosing for alendronate/risedronate and monthly oral dosing for ibandronate — an important consideration for patients with adherence challenges.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In Figure 8, teriparatide and romosozumab sit on the "bone formation" side of the balance, while alendronate and raloxifene sit on the "bone resorption" side. What does this grouping represent?

options.A: Teriparatide and romosozumab stimulate osteoblast activity, while alendronate and raloxifene inhibit osteoclast activity
options.B: All four drugs work through the identical mechanism
options.C: Teriparatide and romosozumab inhibit osteoclasts, while alendronate and raloxifene stimulate osteoblasts
options.D: This grouping reflects route of administration, not mechanism

items.why: The "anabolic" agents (teriparatide, abaloparatide, romosozumab) sit on the bone-formation side because they stimulate osteoblasts, while bisphosphonates (alendronate), denosumab, SERMs (raloxifene), and calcitonin sit on the bone-resorption side because they inhibit osteoclasts — two different strategies for shifting the same remodeling balance.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient is counseled to take their oral bisphosphonate with a full glass of water and remain upright for a specified period. What complication is this counseling primarily meant to prevent?
items.why: Taking the tablet with a full glass of water and staying upright reduces the time the pill is in contact with the esophageal mucosa, lowering the risk of esophageal irritation or injury.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with osteoporosis has significant difficulty swallowing pills. Which administration route among osteoporosis therapies would best fit this patient?

options.C: There is no alternative to oral bisphosphonates
options.D: Yearly IV zoledronic acid or a subcutaneous injectable agent

items.why: Route of administration and adherence are explicit factors in choosing osteoporosis therapy — IV zoledronic acid or an injectable agent (e.g., denosumab) avoids the swallowing difficulty that limits oral options.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why is acetaminophen not a reliable first-line choice for an inflammatory joint flare, despite being a good analgesic/antipyretic?

options.B: It has minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory effect
options.C: It is contraindicated in all patients with joint pain
options.D: It is a DMARD and too strong for mild flares

items.why: Acetaminophen has minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory effect, unlike NSAIDs — it treats pain and fever, not inflammation itself.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 70-year-old with CKD and heart failure needs osteoarthritis pain control. Considering systemic risk, which is generally the safest starting point?
items.why: Acetaminophen or a topical NSAID avoids the systemic renal/CV risk of oral NSAIDs in a patient with CKD and heart failure.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which pairing correctly matches a drug with its primary mechanism?

options.C: Baclofen — calcium channel blockade in skeletal muscle

items.why: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase; colchicine disrupts microtubules; baclofen is a GABA-B agonist.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on a biologic DMARD develops a fever. What is the most important immediate concern?

options.A: Infection, given the drug’s immunosuppressive effect

items.why: Immunosuppression is the shared major risk across all DMARDs — a fever must be treated as a possible infection until proven otherwise.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which statement about gout pharmacology is correct?

options.B: Acute flares should always be treated with urate-lowering therapy first
options.C: Probenecid lowers uric acid by inhibiting renal tubular reabsorption of urate
options.D: Febuxostat and probenecid are both xanthine oxidase inhibitors

items.why: Probenecid is a uricosuric agent that inhibits renal tubular reabsorption of uric acid, increasing its excretion. Colchicine does not lower uric acid; febuxostat (not probenecid) is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor; and urate-lowering therapy is deferred during an acute flare.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis risk should be counseled that the risk is primarily related to which mechanism?

options.A: Increased osteoclast-mediated resorption and decreased bone formation

items.why: Glucocorticoids increase osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and suppress osteoblast-driven bone formation — shifting the remodeling balance toward bone loss.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: How does colchicine relieve an acute gout flare?

options.A: It disrupts microtubules, reducing neutrophil migration
options.B: It blocks phospholipase A₂ upstream of COX
options.C: It converts uric acid to allantoin in the joint
options.D: It blocks URAT1, increasing uric acid excretion
options.E: It inhibits xanthine oxidase, lowering uric acid

items.why: Colchicine binds tubulin and blocks microtubule polymerization, reducing neutrophil migration and NLRP3 activation (S10; S11; SG U2-M).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on colchicine for a gout flare is prescribed clarithromycin for pneumonia. What is the concern?

options.A: Clarithromycin speeds colchicine clearance, so the flare returns
options.C: CYP3A4/P-gp inhibition raises colchicine to toxic levels
options.D: The pair raises uric acid and worsens the flare
options.E: The two together cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency

items.why: CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibitors such as clarithromycin, cyclosporine, and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors raise colchicine toxicity (S11).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient of Han Chinese descent with recurrent gout is about to start allopurinol. Which pre-treatment step does the lecture tie to Lecture 1’s pharmacogenomics?

options.A: G6PD testing for hemolysis risk on the drug
options.B: HLA-B*58:01 testing for severe hypersensitivity risk
options.C: TPMT testing for bone marrow toxicity risk
options.D: CYP2D6 genotyping for poor metabolizer status
options.E: Baseline joint aspiration for urate crystals

items.why: The HLA-B*58:01 allele raises the risk of severe cutaneous/hypersensitivity reactions to allopurinol (S12; S13); the textbook recommends screening in Han Chinese, Korean, and Thai patients (p. 696).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with refractory tophaceous gout is being considered for pegloticase. Which test must come first?

options.C: A 24-hour urine urate, to rule out stones
options.E: G6PD activity, because of hemolysis risk

items.why: Pegloticase and rasburicase are contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (hemolysis risk) (S15).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with gout and CKD stage 3 is starting allopurinol. Which textbook starting dose fits?

options.A: Allopurinol is not used at all in CKD
options.B: 300 mg/d from day one to reach target fast
options.C: 100 mg/d, the same as normal kidney function
options.D: No more than 50 mg/d, titrated by 50 mg

items.why: In chronic kidney disease the initial allopurinol dose should not exceed 50 mg/d, with 50-mg titrations (p. 695).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: During general anesthesia with a volatile agent and succinylcholine, a patient develops rising temperature, rigidity, and acidosis. Which drug is the emergency treatment, and where does it act?

options.A: Baclofen, activating GABA-B receptors in the cord
options.C: Dantrolene, blocking RyR1 calcium release in muscle

items.why: Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine; dantrolene blocks RyR1 so less calcium leaves the sarcoplasmic reticulum (S34; S35; SG U2-R11).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with multiple sclerosis has an intrathecal baclofen pump. The pump runs dry over a holiday weekend. What should the team anticipate?

options.A: Serotonin syndrome from loss of 5-HT2 block
options.B: No change, since baclofen has a long half-life
options.D: Rebound hypertension from loss of α2 action

items.why: Abrupt discontinuation, especially intrathecal, can cause a dangerous withdrawal syndrome with seizures, hyperthermia, and rebound spasticity (S27; S28).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient taking tizanidine for spasticity is prescribed ciprofloxacin for a urinary infection. What is the problem?

options.A: Ciprofloxacin blocks RyR1 and adds weakness
options.C: Ciprofloxacin induces CYP1A2, so spasticity returns
options.E: CYP1A2 inhibition sharply raises tizanidine levels

items.why: Ciprofloxacin and fluvoxamine strongly raise tizanidine levels via CYP1A2 — the combination is contraindicated (S30).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 78-year-old asks for cyclobenzaprine for back spasm. Which concern is most specific to this drug in an older adult?

options.C: Seizures on abrupt withdrawal of a pump
options.E: Hemolysis in a patient with G6PD deficiency

items.why: Cyclobenzaprine is tricyclic-like: dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, confusion — on the Beers list in older adults; short-term use only (S31; S32).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which agent is a Schedule IV controlled substance because it is metabolized to meprobamate?
items.why: Carisoprodol is metabolized to meprobamate and is a Schedule IV controlled substance with dependence/misuse potential (S33).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A young man with extensive burns needs emergency intubation. Why is succinylcholine avoided?

options.A: It lasts many hours in burned patients
options.B: Potassium release can cause cardiac arrest
options.C: It cannot reach the burned muscle tissue
options.D: Burns make it a nondepolarizing blocker
options.E: It is reversed too quickly by sugammadex

items.why: Burns and denervation proliferate extrajunctional receptors; succinylcholine then releases potassium, which can cause cardiac arrest (p. 508).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 66-year-old woman starts weekly alendronate. Which counseling point most reduces her risk of esophageal injury?

options.A: Take it with breakfast to protect the stomach
options.B: Take it at bedtime with a calcium supplement
options.C: Lie down for 30 minutes after the dose
options.D: Take it with coffee to speed gastric emptying
options.E: Full glass of plain water, then stay upright 30 minutes

items.why: Take with a full glass of water first thing in the morning, fasting, and remain upright — this reduces esophageal contact time and irritation (S52; S53; SG U2-R13).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which option correctly describes the PTH feedback loop?

options.A: Low calcium → vitamin D → PTH suppression and calcium excretion
options.B: High calcium → PTH → bone formation, renal excretion, less gut absorption
options.C: Low calcium → PTH → bone resorption, renal reabsorption, vitamin D gut absorption
options.D: Low calcium → calcitonin → bone resorption and renal reabsorption
options.E: Low calcium → PTH → osteoblast-only bone formation

items.why: Falling calcium triggers PTH, which raises calcium via bone resorption, renal reabsorption, and (via vitamin D activation) intestinal absorption (S43; SG U2-R12).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which osteoporosis drug is an anabolic PTH analog that stimulates osteoblast bone formation?
items.why: Teriparatide (PTH 1-34, daily injection) is an anabolic agent that stimulates osteoblasts and new bone formation (S54; S55; SG U2-M).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on denosumab for 4 years wants to stop it because of the injections. What should the PA advise?

options.B: Take a drug holiday, as for bisphosphonates
options.D: Don’t just stop — transition to a bisphosphonate
options.E: Stop safely: its effect lasts years in bone

items.why: Denosumab discontinuation causes rebound vertebral fractures; transition to a bisphosphonate (S55).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 70-year-old with a myocardial infarction 6 months ago has severe osteoporosis. Which agent should be avoided because of its boxed warning?
items.why: Romosozumab carries a boxed warning for MI, stroke, and cardiovascular death (S55).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with CrCl 25 mL/min has osteoporosis. Which drug class is contraindicated at this kidney function?
items.why: Bisphosphonates are contraindicated with severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30–35 mL/min) (S48); renal function is part of choosing therapy (S59).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why does raloxifene suit some patients with vertebral osteoporosis but not those whose main risk is hip fracture?

options.A: It is contraindicated in all women over 65
options.B: It must be stopped after 2 years
options.C: It builds new bone only in the hip
options.D: It raises hip fracture risk through VTE
options.E: It reduces spine fractures but not hip fractures

items.why: Raloxifene protects against spine fractures but not hip fractures, unlike bisphosphonates, denosumab, and teriparatide (p. 827).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 72-year-old with OA, CKD, hypertension, and an anticoagulant now has an acute gout flare. Which plan best fits the study guide?

options.B: Start febuxostat today to stop the flare
options.C: Probenecid now, since the kidneys are the issue
options.D: Full-dose oral naproxen; start allopurinol now

items.why: An oral NSAID is relatively contraindicated (CKD, anticoagulant, hypertension); a short corticosteroid course is often preferred, colchicine needs renal dose adjustment, and ULT waits until the flare resolves (SG U2-S).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which mechanism belongs to baclofen?

options.A: GABA-B agonism in the spinal cord

items.why: Baclofen activates GABA-B receptors, causing presynaptic inhibition and less excitatory transmitter release.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 68-year-old woman with prior vertebral fractures and very high fracture risk is choosing therapy. What does the lecture suggest first?

options.A: A drug holiday from all therapy

items.why: Higher-risk patients may need an anabolic agent first (then an antiresorptive); fracture history, renal function, and route also guide choice.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 76-year-old with benign prostatic hyperplasia asks for a muscle relaxant for a back strain. Why is cyclobenzaprine a poor fit?

options.A: It blocks RyR1 and causes profound weakness
options.C: It causes hemolysis in older adults with BPH
options.D: It requires routine liver enzyme monitoring with use
options.E: It is only effective given intrathecally

items.why: Cyclobenzaprine is tricyclic-like: dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, confusion — on the Beers list for older adults.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Ten days after starting allopurinol, a patient develops a rash and fever. A severe cutaneous reaction is suspected. How is this reaction best classified?

options.A: Type B (idiosyncratic) reaction — stop allopurinol at once
options.B: Type A (augmented) reaction — lower the dose and continue
options.C: A drug–drug interaction with prophylactic colchicine
options.D: Expected therapeutic effect of lowering uric acid
options.E: Toxicity from levels above the therapeutic range

items.why: Allopurinol hypersensitivity (SJS/TEN, linked to HLA-B*58:01) is unpredictable and not dose-related; the textbook says stop at the first sign of a rash.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which urate-lowering drug carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death?
items.why: Febuxostat carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death (the textbook notes later data were reassuring; answer with the slides).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman with a past DVT asks about raloxifene for osteoporosis. What is the key concern?

options.A: It must be taken upright with water
options.C: It causes osteonecrosis of the jaw
options.E: It carries a boxed MI and stroke warning

items.why: Raloxifene raises VTE risk (and causes hot flashes), though it may reduce breast cancer risk.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A transplant patient taking azathioprine with known intermediate TPMT activity now needs urate-lowering therapy. Which plan is safest?

options.A: Allopurinol at full dose with no change to azathioprine
options.B: Allopurinol with a large azathioprine dose cut and CBC checks
options.C: Probenecid alone, since TPMT status never matters
options.D: Double the azathioprine dose to offset its faster clearance
options.E: No change needed, because TPMT only affects allopurinol

items.why: Allopurinol raises azathioprine/mercaptopurine exposure (reduce the dose — textbook: by 75%), and low TPMT already raises myelosuppression risk.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with osteoporosis has achalasia and cannot stay upright after taking tablets. Which option best addresses both problems?

options.A: Yearly IV zoledronic acid or a subcutaneous injectable
options.B: No therapy, since all osteoporosis drugs are oral
options.C: Weekly oral alendronate with extra water
options.D: Monthly oral ibandronate taken at bedtime

items.why: Avoid oral bisphosphonates in esophageal stricture, achalasia, or inability to sit upright; IV zoledronic acid or an injectable (e.g., denosumab) avoids the oral route.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on prednisone 10 mg daily for 2 years asks why bone density is falling. Which explanation is correct?

options.A: Bone loss only happens at doses above 60 mg
options.B: Glucocorticoids raise calcitonin and lower PTH
options.C: More resorption and less bone formation
options.D: Too much osteoblast stimulation by the steroid

items.why: Chronic glucocorticoids increase osteoclast resorption and suppress osteoblast formation (and, per the textbook, cut gut calcium absorption) — a key osteoporosis risk factor.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with multiple sclerosis and stage 4 CKD needs baclofen for spasticity. Which plan best reflects safe prescribing?

options.A: Standard dosing, since baclofen is cleared by the liver
options.B: A loading dose to reach steady state faster
options.C: Avoid every centrally acting drug in kidney disease
options.D: Stop it abruptly if any sedation appears
options.E: Use a reduced dose with slow titration and monitor for sedation

items.why: Baclofen requires renal dose adjustment; reduced clearance raises CNS depression risk, and it must be tapered, not stopped abruptly.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman with a past DVT asks about raloxifene for osteoporosis. What is the key concern?

options.B: It causes osteonecrosis of the jaw
options.D: It carries a boxed MI and stroke warning
options.E: It must be taken upright with water

items.why: Raloxifene raises VTE risk (and causes hot flashes), though it may reduce breast cancer risk.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which mechanism belongs to baclofen?

options.D: GABA-B agonism in the spinal cord

items.why: Baclofen activates GABA-B receptors, causing presynaptic inhibition and less excitatory transmitter release.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which effect explains glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis?

options.D: Excess vitamin D from the kidney

items.why: Glucocorticoids increase osteoclast-mediated resorption and suppress osteoblast-driven formation, tipping the balance to bone loss.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: In a gout flare, what activates the inflammatory response once urate crystals form in the joint?
items.why: Monosodium urate crystals activate neutrophils and macrophages through NLRP3 and IL-1β, producing the acute flare.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on long-term colchicine prophylaxis is admitted for pneumonia and started on clarithromycin. What should the clinician anticipate?

options.A: Lower colchicine levels and a breakthrough gout flare
options.B: No meaningful change, since colchicine is renally cleared only
options.C: Colchicine toxicity; reduce or hold colchicine
options.D: Faster uric acid excretion from the antibiotic
options.E: Hemolysis, so check G6PD before continuing

items.why: CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibitors (clarithromycin, cyclosporine, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors) raise colchicine levels; with its narrow window, toxicity follows.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Falling serum calcium triggers PTH release. Which set lists PTH’s three ways of raising calcium?

options.A: Gut secretion, bone formation, vitamin D breakdown
options.B: Bone formation, renal excretion, gut secretion
options.C: Renal excretion, osteoblast growth, insulin release
options.E: Bone resorption, renal reabsorption, gut absorption

items.why: PTH raises calcium via bone resorption, renal reabsorption, and (via vitamin D activation) intestinal absorption.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: In the OR, a patient develops rising temperature, rigidity, and acidosis after a volatile anesthetic. Which route and drug meet the need for immediate, complete delivery?
items.why: Malignant hyperthermia is treated with IV dantrolene — IV gives the whole dose at once with no absorption step.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient’s first gout flare settled two weeks ago; uric acid remains high and flares are recurring. What is the best next step?

options.A: Give colchicine only until the next flare
options.B: Wait for the next flare before deciding
options.D: Start allopurinol at full dose with no prophylaxis
options.E: Start allopurinol low with colchicine prophylaxis

items.why: Once the flare resolves, start a xanthine oxidase inhibitor low, titrate to a urate target, and give colchicine or an NSAID prophylaxis for 3–6 months.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which urate-lowering drug carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death?
items.why: Febuxostat carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death (the textbook notes later data were reassuring; answer with the slides).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes spasticity from rigidity?

options.A: Both respond to the same drugs
options.C: Spasticity is velocity-dependent; rigidity is not
options.D: Spasticity is a sudden involuntary contraction
options.E: Rigidity is velocity-dependent; spasticity is not

items.why: Spasticity is velocity-dependent increased tone from upper motor neuron injury; rigidity is constant tone, independent of velocity.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 70-year-old with a stroke 8 months ago has very high fracture risk. Which anabolic choice is most defensible?

options.A: No anabolic agent, since all carry a stroke warning
options.B: Raloxifene, which is the strongest anabolic drug
options.C: Romosozumab, since it both builds bone and limits resorption
options.D: Teriparatide or abaloparatide rather than romosozumab
options.E: Calcitonin alone as the first-line anabolic

items.why: Romosozumab carries a boxed warning for MI, stroke, and CV death (textbook: contraindicated after MI or stroke within a year); the PTH analogs are the anabolic alternative (2-year limit).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Ten days after starting allopurinol, a patient develops a rash and fever. A severe cutaneous reaction is suspected. How is this reaction best classified?

options.A: Type B (idiosyncratic) reaction — stop allopurinol at once
options.B: Toxicity from levels above the therapeutic range
options.C: Expected therapeutic effect of lowering uric acid
options.D: Type A (augmented) reaction — lower the dose and continue
options.E: A drug–drug interaction with prophylactic colchicine

items.why: Allopurinol hypersensitivity (SJS/TEN, linked to HLA-B*58:01) is unpredictable and not dose-related; the textbook says stop at the first sign of a rash.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Denosumab has controlled a patient’s osteoporosis for 5 years. The patient now wants to stop all injections. What should the clinician anticipate?

options.A: Improved bone density once the antibody clears
options.B: Rebound vertebral fractures unless a bisphosphonate follows
options.C: No change, since its effect persists in bone for years

items.why: Denosumab blocks osteoclast formation without killing osteoclasts or depositing in bone; stopping causes rebound resorption and vertebral fractures — transition to a bisphosphonate.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 76-year-old with benign prostatic hyperplasia asks for a muscle relaxant for a back strain. Why is cyclobenzaprine a poor fit?

options.A: It causes hemolysis in older adults with BPH
options.C: It requires routine liver enzyme monitoring with use
options.D: It blocks RyR1 and causes profound weakness
options.E: It is only effective given intrathecally

items.why: Cyclobenzaprine is tricyclic-like: dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, confusion — on the Beers list for older adults.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient stable on tizanidine for spasticity is prescribed fluvoxamine. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Avoid the pair — CYP1A2 inhibition raises tizanidine
options.B: Continue both, since tizanidine has a wide therapeutic index
options.C: Increase the tizanidine dose to keep spasticity controlled
options.E: Switch tizanidine to an IV form to bypass the interaction

items.why: Ciprofloxacin and fluvoxamine strongly inhibit CYP1A2, raising tizanidine levels (hypotension, sedation) — the combination is contraindicated.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: What distinguishes dantrolene from cyclobenzaprine, tizanidine, and baclofen?

options.A: It acts on the muscle fiber, not the CNS
options.B: It is a central alpha-2 agonist
options.C: It acts in the brainstem on 5-HT2
options.D: It blocks ACh release at the junction
options.E: It acts on GABA-B receptors in the cord

items.why: Dantrolene decreases calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (RyR1) inside the muscle fiber; the others act in the CNS.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which drug lowers serum uric acid by increasing its renal excretion?
items.why: Probenecid is a uricosuric: it blocks URAT1-mediated tubular reabsorption, so excretion rises.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which osteoporosis drug is limited to 2 years of lifetime use and should be followed by an antiresorptive?
items.why: Teriparatide is limited to 2 years lifetime, then followed by an antiresorptive to keep the bone gained.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on tizanidine reports dizziness on standing and has new elevated liver enzymes. Which pair of effects is typical of tizanidine?
items.why: Tizanidine causes sedation, hypotension/bradycardia, dry mouth, and hepatotoxicity — monitor LFTs.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A trial shows a weekly bisphosphonate prevents fractures, but in practice many patients miss doses because of the strict fasting rules. What does this gap illustrate?

options.A: Poor bioavailability, which IV dosing cannot fix
options.B: The difference between efficacy and effectiveness
options.C: The difference between potency and efficacy
options.D: A Type B adverse drug reaction
options.E: Drug tolerance from long skeletal half-life

items.why: Efficacy is performance under trial conditions; effectiveness is real-world performance with adherence — dosing frequency drives which bisphosphonate patients actually take.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with gout and a history of uric acid kidney stones needs urate-lowering therapy. Which drug should be avoided?
items.why: Probenecid raises urinary uric acid, so avoid it with uric acid kidney stones or significant renal impairment.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which drug blocks osteoclast formation by inhibiting RANKL?
items.why: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL that blocks osteoclast formation (it mimics OPG).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient starting weekly risedronate asks how to take it. Which instruction is correct?

options.A: With an antacid to protect the stomach
options.B: At bedtime, then lie down to rest
options.C: With coffee to help it absorb
options.D: With breakfast and a calcium tablet
options.E: Fasting, full glass of water, upright

items.why: Take it first thing in the morning, fasting, with a full glass of plain water, and stay upright for 30 minutes to limit esophageal irritation.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A transplant patient taking azathioprine develops gout and needs allopurinol. What must happen?

options.B: No change; there is no interaction

items.why: Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase, which clears azathioprine and mercaptopurine — reduce their dose (textbook: by 75%).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 68-year-old woman with prior vertebral fractures and very high fracture risk is choosing therapy. What does the lecture suggest first?

options.D: A drug holiday from all therapy

items.why: Higher-risk patients may need an anabolic agent first (then an antiresorptive); fracture history, renal function, and route also guide choice.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: In the OR, after sevoflurane and succinylcholine, a patient’s end-tidal CO₂ and temperature climb with jaw rigidity. Which drug is given IV now?
items.why: Malignant hyperthermia (volatile anesthetics, succinylcholine) is treated with IV dantrolene, which blocks RyR1 calcium release.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with gout, a recent myocardial infarction, and a mild rash on allopurinol needs a different urate-lowering drug. Why is febuxostat a cautious choice?

options.A: Its boxed CV-death warning, weighed against alternatives
options.B: It is a uricosuric that causes uric acid kidney stones
options.C: It works only during an acute flare
options.D: It cannot lower uric acid at all in any kidney disease
options.E: It must never be combined with any other drug

items.why: Febuxostat is the alternative when allopurinol isn’t tolerated, but it carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death — a risk–benefit judgment against other options.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient taking sertraline is prescribed cyclobenzaprine for a back strain. What interaction should the PA flag?
items.why: Cyclobenzaprine carries serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs, SNRIs, and tramadol; MAOIs are contraindicated.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Before starting pegloticase for refractory gout, which test is essential and why?
items.why: Pegloticase (uricase) has boxed warnings for anaphylaxis, infusion reactions, and hemolysis and methemoglobinemia in G6PD deficiency. Premedicate, stop other urate-lowering drugs and monitor serum urate.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 70-year-old with severe osteoporosis and prior pelvic radiation for cervical cancer is considered for an anabolic drug. Which is the problem?

options.B: Raloxifene is the anabolic of choice
options.C: Teriparatide must be given IV yearly
options.D: Prior skeletal radiation rules out teriparatide
options.E: Teriparatide is limited to a 6-month lifetime course

items.why: Teriparatide (PTH 1–34 analog, 20 mcg SC daily, 2-year lifetime limit) is contraindicated with Paget disease, prior skeletal radiation, bone metastases, hypercalcemia and open epiphyses; follow with an antiresorptive to keep gains.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient's first gout flare settled 3 weeks ago; urate is 9.2 mg/dL and he has had 3 flares this year. Allopurinol is started. What should accompany it for the first months?

options.A: Probenecid during the first flare that occurs
options.B: Nothing; allopurinol prevents flares from day one
options.D: Stop allopurinol if a flare occurs
options.E: Colchicine 0.6 mg once or twice daily

items.why: Urate-lowering therapy mobilizes urate and triggers flares at initiation; colchicine 0.6 mg once or twice daily is used as prophylaxis while titrating. If a flare occurs, treat it and continue the allopurinol.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 74-year-old on sertraline and tramadol has an acute back spasm. She drives and lives alone. Which relaxant is the poorest choice?

options.C: Baclofen at a low starting dose

items.why: Cyclobenzaprine is tricyclic-related: anticholinergic, sedating, on the Beers list for older adults, and risks serotonin syndrome with SSRIs and tramadol.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 52-year-old of Han Chinese ancestry with recurrent gout and an eGFR of 45 is starting allopurinol. Which plan is best?

options.A: HLA-B*58:01 test, low start, urate goal < 6
options.D: Start during the current flare to stop it
options.E: Skip flare prophylaxis; flares won't happen

items.why: Allopurinol: start 50–100 mg daily and titrate every 2–5 weeks to serum urate under 6 mg/dL; reduce dose in renal impairment; HLA-B*58:01 carriers (higher in some Asian ancestries) are at higher risk of severe hypersensitivity; flares at initiation need prophylaxis.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with osteoporosis has taken denosumab for 6 years and wants to stop all treatment. Compared with stopping a bisphosphonate after 6 years, what is different?

options.A: Both should simply be stopped after 5 years
options.B: No difference; both keep working for years
options.D: Stopping a bisphosphonate causes the rebound
options.E: Denosumab protects longer because it is an antibody

items.why: Bisphosphonates bind bone and are retained for months to years (hence a drug holiday). Denosumab does not deposit in bone: stopping or missing doses causes a surge of resorption and multiple vertebral fractures — transition to a bisphosphonate.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with multiple sclerosis and stage 4 CKD takes baclofen 20 mg three times daily and is newly drowsy and confused. What is the most likely explanation and response?

options.E: Renal accumulation; reduce the dose gradually

items.why: Baclofen is renally cleared: caution in renal impairment (sedation, confusion, coma in overdose). Never stop abruptly — withdrawal causes seizures, hyperthermia and rebound spasticity — so taper.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 66-year-old with stage 4 CKD takes clarithromycin for pneumonia and now has an acute gout flare in the knee. Which flare treatment is best?

options.A: Colchicine 1.2 mg, then 0.6 mg an hour later

items.why: Colchicine is contraindicated with severe renal impairment plus CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors like clarithromycin (narrow therapeutic window, fatal toxicity). Corticosteroids are the taught alternative when NSAIDs or colchicine are contraindicated, including CKD.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 78-year-old with osteoporosis has a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min. Which therapy best fits her kidney function?

options.D: Alendronate 10 mg daily instead of weekly
options.E: Denosumab 60 mg SC every 6 months, watching calcium

items.why: Alendronate and zoledronic acid are avoided when CrCl is below 35 mL/min. Denosumab is not renally cleared and can be used in advanced renal disease — watch for hypocalcemia.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A kidney-transplant patient on azathioprine had a myocardial infarction last year. She needs urate-lowering therapy. Which drug is the worst choice for her?

options.C: Allopurinol with an azathioprine dose cut

items.why: Febuxostat is contraindicated with azathioprine or mercaptopurine and carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death — two strikes for this patient.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: An 80-kg patient develops malignant hyperthermia after sevoflurane and succinylcholine. What is the correct initial dantrolene dose?

options.C: 800 mg IV as a single first dose
options.D: 200 mg IV (2.5 mg/kg), repeated up to 10 mg/kg

items.why: Dantrolene blocks RyR1 calcium release in muscle. MH: 2.5 mg/kg IV (80 kg → 200 mg), repeat up to 10 mg/kg. Oral use carries a hepatotoxicity boxed warning; caution with calcium channel blockers (IV).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman on raloxifene for osteoporosis is scheduled for knee replacement with several days of immobility. What is the key counseling point?

options.A: Stop raloxifene before the period of immobilization
options.B: Double the dose to protect the new joint
options.C: Hot flashes are the main surgical risk
options.D: Continue it; it protects against hip fracture

items.why: Raloxifene (SERM): boxed warning for VTE and death from stroke; stop before prolonged immobilization. It reduces spine (not hip) fractures and lowers invasive breast cancer risk.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on tizanidine for spasticity starts ciprofloxacin for a UTI. Two days later his BP is 84/50 and HR 48, and he is very drowsy. What happened?
items.why: Tizanidine (central alpha-2 agonist) is contraindicated with strong CYP1A2 inhibitors (ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine): levels rise → hypotension, bradycardia, CNS depression. Check liver tests.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: The day after her first zoledronic acid infusion, a woman has fever, muscle aches and fatigue. Her calcium was replete beforehand. What is the best explanation?

options.E: Osteonecrosis of the jaw from the infusion

items.why: Zoledronic acid (IV yearly): flu-like acute-phase reaction, hypocalcemia, renal injury and ONJ; hydrate and replete calcium and vitamin D first; avoid with CrCl below 35.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with RA on weekly methotrexate is started on probenecid for gout. Which effect should the clinician anticipate?

options.B: Lower methotrexate levels and RA flares
options.D: Lower penicillin levels if she needs one

items.why: Probenecid (URAT1 inhibitor) raises levels of penicillins, methotrexate and NSAIDs; it also causes kidney stones (hydrate, alkalinize urine) and is avoided with eGFR under 30 or during a flare.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 72-year-old woman with very high fracture risk had a stroke 7 months ago. Romosozumab is being discussed. What is the correct decision?

options.A: Use it with aspirin for protection
options.C: Use it since it is antiresorptive only
options.D: Use it; the stroke was over 6 months ago
options.E: Avoid: stroke within the past year

items.why: Romosozumab (sclerostin antibody) carries a boxed warning: contraindicated after MI or stroke within the past year. Given 210 mg SC monthly for one year, then an antiresorptive.

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Acid-peptic disease reflects an imbalance between mucosal defense and aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs).

items.label: Definition
items.text: Acid-peptic disease is a balance between mucosal defense and acid-driven aggression.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Aggressive factors: gastric acid (HCl), pepsin, H. pylori infection, NSAID use (suppresses protective prostaglandins).
items.back: gastric acid (HCl), pepsin, H. pylori infection, NSAID use (suppresses protective prostaglandins).
items.cloze: {{c1::Aggressive factors}}: gastric acid (HCl), pepsin, H. pylori infection, NSAID use (suppresses protective prostaglandins).

items.label: Definition
items.text: Protective (mucosal defense) factors: mucus–bicarbonate layer; prostaglandins (stimulate mucus/bicarbonate, maintain mucosal blood flow); epithelial cell turnover.
items.back: mucus–bicarbonate layer; prostaglandins (stimulate mucus/bicarbonate, maintain mucosal blood flow); epithelial cell turnover.
items.cloze: {{c1::Protective (mucosal defense) factors}}: mucus–bicarbonate layer; prostaglandins (stimulate mucus/bicarbonate, maintain mucosal blood flow); epithelial cell turnover.

items.label: Definition
items.text: GERD: reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, causing heartburn/regurgitation and, over time, esophageal mucosal injury.
items.back: reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, causing heartburn/regurgitation and, over time, esophageal mucosal injury.
items.cloze: {{c1::GERD}}: reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, causing heartburn/regurgitation and, over time, esophageal mucosal injury.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Peptic ulcer disease (PUD): a break in the mucosa of the stomach or duodenum; most commonly caused by H. pylori infection or NSAID use.
items.back: a break in the mucosa of the stomach or duodenum; most commonly caused by H. pylori infection or NSAID use.
items.cloze: {{c1::Peptic ulcer disease (PUD)}}: a break in the mucosa of the stomach or duodenum; most commonly caused by H. pylori infection or NSAID use.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Gastritis: inflammation of the gastric mucosa — acute (e.g., NSAID- or alcohol-related) or chronic (e.g., H. pylori-driven).
items.back: inflammation of the gastric mucosa — acute (e.g., NSAID- or alcohol-related) or chronic (e.g., H. pylori-driven).
items.cloze: {{c1::Gastritis}}: inflammation of the gastric mucosa — acute (e.g., NSAID- or alcohol-related) or chronic (e.g., H. pylori-driven).

items.label: Definition
items.text: Over 90% of peptic ulcers are caused by H. pylori infection or NSAIDs; bile also counts as an aggressive factor.
items.cloze: Over {{c1::90%}} of peptic ulcers are caused by H. pylori infection or NSAIDs; bile also counts as an aggressive factor.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: GERD, PUD and gastritis share the same drug toolkit: reduce acid, protect the mucosa, and/or eradicate H. pylori.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: H. pylori and NSAIDs cause most PUD.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: H2RAs block only the histamine input; gastrin and acetylcholine still drive the pump — PPIs block the final common pathway regardless of which input is active.
items.cloze: H2RAs block only the histamine input; gastrin and acetylcholine still drive the pump … {{c1::PPIs block the final common pathway regardless of which input is active}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Disease appears when aggressive factors win or defenses fall: aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) overwhelm mucus, bicarbonate and prostaglandin-driven blood flow → mucosal injury → GERD, ulcer or gastritis.
items.front: Disease appears when aggressive factors win or defenses fall
items.back: aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) overwhelm mucus, bicarbonate and prostaglandin-driven blood flow → mucosal injury → GERD, ulcer or gastritis.
items.cloze: Disease appears when aggressive factors win or defenses fall: {{c1::aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H}}. pylori, NSAIDs) overwhelm mucus, bicarbonate and prostaglandin-driven blood flow → mucosal injury → GERD, ulcer or gastritis.

items.label: How it works
items.text: NSAIDs block COX-1 prostaglandins, removing mucosal protection — the clearest example of tipping the balance.
items.front: NSAIDs block COX-1 prostaglandins, removing mucosal protection …
items.back: the clearest example of tipping the balance.
items.cloze: {{c1::NSAIDs block COX-1 prostaglandins}}, removing mucosal protection — the clearest example of tipping the balance.

items.label: How it works
items.text: H. pylori urease makes ammonia, which injures the mucosa.
items.cloze: {{c1::H. pylori urease makes ammonia}}, which injures the mucosa.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Stress and critical illness raise the risk of stress ulceration.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison) causes severe acid hypersecretion.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine all converge on the parietal cell proton pump. H2 blockers cut one input (histamine); PPIs block the last step itself.
items.cloze: {{c1::Gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine all converge on the parietal cell proton pump}}. H2 blockers cut one input (histamine); PPIs block the last step itself.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Physiology of acid secretion: gastrin acts mainly by releasing histamine from ECL cells; acetylcholine (M3) stimulates the parietal cell directly; somatostatin from antral D cells turns gastrin off.
items.back: gastrin acts mainly by releasing histamine from ECL cells; acetylcholine (M3) stimulates the parietal cell directly; somatostatin from antral D cells turns gastrin off.
items.cloze: {{c1::Physiology of acid secretion}}: gastrin acts mainly by releasing histamine from ECL cells; acetylcholine (M3) stimulates the parietal cell directly; somatostatin from antral D cells turns gastrin off.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why do NSAIDs cause ulcers? They block the COX-1 prostaglandins that make mucus and bicarbonate and keep mucosal blood flow up — they take the defense away.

items.text: Three keys, one lock: gastrin, histamine, ACh all turn the pump; PPIs change the lock.

items.text: PPIs block the parietal cell’s final common pathway and are the most potent antisecretory agents, but carry real long-term risks (B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, fracture, C. difficile).

items.text: Antacids: fast, short, don’t reduce production; separate other drugs by 2 hours.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why before breakfast? PPIs only hit pumps that are actively secreting; a meal switches pumps on, so the drug should be peaking when they turn on.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why does PPI use cause B12 deficiency? Acid frees B12 from food protein; less acid, less B12 released.
