items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Based on Figure 1, why do PPIs achieve more complete acid suppression than H2 receptor antagonists?

options.A: PPIs block the final common pathway (the proton pump itself), so they work regardless of which upstream signal is driving acid secretion
options.B: PPIs block only the gastrin pathway, which is the strongest stimulus
options.C: H2RAs block the proton pump directly, while PPIs act upstream
options.D: There is no mechanistic difference between the two classes

items.why: H2RAs block only one of three inputs to the parietal cell (histamine), so gastrin and acetylcholine can still drive acid secretion. PPIs irreversibly inhibit the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump — the single convergence point for all three signals — producing more complete and longer-lasting acid suppression.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient taking clopidogrel after a cardiac stent is started on omeprazole for GERD. What is the primary concern with this combination?

options.A: Omeprazole may reduce CYP2C19-mediated activation of clopidogrel, blunting its antiplatelet effect
options.B: Omeprazole increases clopidogrel absorption, raising bleeding risk
options.C: There is no clinically relevant interaction between these two drugs
options.D: Omeprazole should never be combined with any cardiac medication

items.why: Clopidogrel is a prodrug that requires CYP2C19 activation. Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, which can reduce clopidogrel’s active metabolite and blunt its antiplatelet effect — a clinically important interaction, especially soon after stent placement.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient is started on misoprostol for NSAID-induced ulcer prevention. What is the single most important question to ask before prescribing?

options.A: Is the patient taking any antacids?
options.B: Is there any possibility of pregnancy?
options.C: Does the patient have a penicillin allergy?
options.D: Is the patient on a PPI already?

items.why: Misoprostol is a potent uterotonic and is contraindicated in pregnancy due to abortifacient risk — pregnancy status must be ruled out (and reliable contraception confirmed) before starting therapy.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with motion sickness needs prophylaxis before a cruise. Based on Figure 9, which drug class targets the pathway most relevant to this cause of nausea?

options.A: H1 / M1 antagonists (e.g., meclizine, scopolamine) — targeting the vestibular system
options.C: NK1 antagonists (e.g., aprepitant) — targeting the CTZ
options.D: D2 antagonists (e.g., metoclopramide) — targeting the CTZ

items.why: Motion sickness is driven primarily by vestibular system input, which signals through histamine (H1) and muscarinic (M1) receptors — exactly the pathway meclizine and scopolamine block in Figure 9. The other classes target gut/chemo (5-HT3) or CTZ (D2, NK1) inputs, which are not the primary driver here.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient has been on metoclopramide for gastroparesis for several months. What is the primary long-term safety concern that should limit duration of therapy?
items.why: Metoclopramide carries a boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia, with risk increasing with duration of use and cumulative dose — therapy should generally be limited to the shortest effective duration (typically no more than 12 weeks).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which set lists only protective (mucosal defense) factors?
items.why: Protective factors are the mucus–bicarbonate layer, prostaglandins, and epithelial cell turnover (S5; SG U3-R1).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma), what drives the ulcer disease?

options.B: Severe acid hypersecretion from excess gastrin
options.D: Loss of COX-1 prostaglandins from NSAID use
options.E: Reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus

items.why: Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison) causes severe acid hypersecretion (S6).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which statement describes how PPIs work?

options.A: Bases that neutralize acid already in the stomach
options.B: PGE1 analogs that raise mucus and bicarbonate
options.C: Polymers that coat the ulcer base in acid
options.D: Acid-activated prodrugs that covalently block the proton pump
options.E: Competitive blockers of histamine at the H2 receptor

items.why: PPIs are enteric-coated prodrugs activated by acid in the canaliculus that bind the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase covalently until new pumps are made (S15–S16).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on long-term omeprazole asks what to monitor. Which set reflects the class-wide long-term risks?

options.D: Serum potassium and digoxin level only
options.E: B12, magnesium, fracture risk, C. difficile

items.why: Long-term PPI risks: B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, fractures, C. difficile (plus pneumonia, interstitial nephritis) (S15–S16; SG U3-R3).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient taking levothyroxine starts calcium carbonate for heartburn. What counseling is needed?

options.A: Switch to cimetidine to avoid any interaction
options.B: Take them together to improve absorption
options.C: Separate the doses by at least 2 hours
options.D: No counseling — antacids act only locally

items.why: Antacids impair absorption of many oral drugs, including levothyroxine and quinolones — separate by at least 2 hours (S12; S53; S71).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: An 82-year-old with CKD on famotidine becomes confused. What is the likely explanation?

options.B: Hypomagnesemia from long-term H2 blocker use
options.C: Milk-alkali syndrome from the H2 blocker
options.D: Cimetidine-like CYP inhibition raising other drugs
options.E: Famotidine accumulated without renal dose adjustment

items.why: Famotidine needs renal dose adjustment and can cause confusion in older adults with renal impairment (S13 notes; S14; S51).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which antacid is most likely to cause diarrhea and accumulate in renal impairment?
items.why: Magnesium hydroxide can cause diarrhea; use caution in renal impairment because magnesium accumulates (S12; S54).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on clopidogrel after a stent needs long-term acid suppression. Which PPI does the textbook prefer?

options.B: Cimetidine, since it is not a PPI
options.E: Any PPI — none interact with clopidogrel

items.why: When PPIs are prescribed with clopidogrel, agents with minimal CYP2C19 inhibition (pantoprazole or rabeprazole) may be preferred (p. 1161).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient needs chronic NSAIDs and has had an NSAID ulcer. How does misoprostol protect, and what is its major contraindication?

options.A: Blocks H2 receptors; avoid in older adults
options.B: Neutralizes acid; separate from other drugs
options.C: PGE1 analog restoring prostaglandin defense; never in pregnancy
options.D: Forms a barrier over the ulcer base; avoid in CKD
options.E: Blocks the proton pump; avoid with clopidogrel

items.why: Misoprostol, a PGE1 analog, restores the prostaglandin tone NSAIDs suppress; it is contraindicated in pregnancy (abortifacient) (S20; SG U3-R5).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient finishes H. pylori therapy and wants a test of cure next week while still on the PPI. What is the right advice?

options.A: Repeat the full regimen without testing
options.B: Test during therapy to adjust antibiotics
options.C: No testing is ever needed after therapy
options.D: Test now; the PPI improves test accuracy
options.E: Test ≥ 4 weeks after therapy, PPI held 2 weeks

items.why: Confirm eradication at least 4 weeks after therapy and off the PPI for 2 weeks — PPIs cause false negatives (S23; S24).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on simvastatin is about to start clarithromycin-based triple therapy. What is the concern?

options.A: CYP3A4 inhibition raises the statin level
options.E: The PPI binds simvastatin in the gut

items.why: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and must not be combined with simvastatin, lovastatin, or ergotamine (S24; S60; S71).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on metronidazole for H. pylori plans to drink wine at a wedding. What should they be told?

options.A: Stop the PPI on the day of drinking
options.B: Avoid alcohol — a disulfiram-like reaction can occur
options.C: Alcohol is fine; only tetracycline interacts
options.D: Take the dose with milk to prevent problems

items.why: Metronidazole plus alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction; avoid alcohol during and for 3 days after (S24; S61).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why must sucralfate be separated from PPIs and antacids?

options.A: It irreversibly blocks the proton pump itself
options.B: It is a PGE1 analog that needs alkaline pH
options.C: It needs an acidic environment to polymerize and bind
options.D: It neutralizes the antacid in the stomach
options.E: It inhibits CYP2C19, raising the PPI level

items.why: Sucralfate polymerizes in acid (pH below 4) to bind the ulcer base; give on an empty stomach, separated from antacids/PPIs (S20–S21).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which pairing correctly matches an antiemetic with its target?
items.why: Aprepitant blocks NK1; ondansetron 5-HT3; meclizine H1/M1; metoclopramide D2 (S30; SG U3-M).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with diabetic gastroparesis has taken metoclopramide for 6 months and now has involuntary lip-smacking movements. What explains this?

options.A: Acute dystonia that resolves with time

items.why: Metoclopramide carries a boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use or high doses; avoid beyond 12 weeks (S36–S37; SG U3-R8).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on citalopram and with a borderline long QT needs an antiemetic after surgery. Why is ondansetron a cautious choice?

options.D: QT prolongation and serotonin syndrome risk

items.why: Ondansetron prolongs the QT interval and carries serotonin syndrome risk with serotonergic drugs (S31).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with refractory chemotherapy nausea is started on dronabinol. How does it work?

options.A: Activates CB1 receptors in the vomiting center and CTZ
options.B: Blocks substance P at NK1 receptors
options.C: Blocks muscarinic receptors in the vestibular system
options.E: Blocks D2 in the chemoreceptor trigger zone

items.why: Dronabinol is a CB1 agonist that reduces neurotransmitter release and stimulates appetite — distinct from 5-HT3, D2, NK1, H1/M1 (S38–S39; SG U3-M).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why are meclizine and scopolamine the classes that fit motion sickness?

options.A: They activate CB1 receptors in the cortex
options.B: They block D2 receptors in the CTZ
options.C: They block 5-HT3 on gut vagal afferents
options.D: They block NK1 receptors in the CTZ
options.E: They block H1/M1 input from the vestibular system

items.why: Motion sickness is vestibular; H1/M1 antagonists block histamine/acetylcholine from the vestibular system (S30; S33 notes; SG U3-R7).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with H. pylori has a penicillin allergy and took azithromycin last year. Best regimen?
items.why: Penicillin allergy rules out amoxicillin; prior macrolide exposure raises clarithromycin-resistance concern.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which factor tips the mucosal balance toward injury by removing prostaglandin protection?
items.why: NSAIDs block COX-1 prostaglandins that drive mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow, tipping the balance toward aggression.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient takes omeprazole at bedtime with no benefit. What counseling best improves its effect?

options.A: Take it with a calcium tablet at night
options.B: Double the dose and keep bedtime timing
options.C: Take it 30–60 minutes before the first meal
options.D: Crush the tablet and take it with milk

items.why: PPIs work best on actively secreting pumps; dosing 30–60 minutes before the first meal matches peak pump activity.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which adverse effect is most associated with ondansetron?
items.why: Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3; it can prolong QT; CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers may respond less.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with confirmed H. pylori took azithromycin for bronchitis 2 months ago and has no drug allergies. Which regimen is preferred?
items.why: Recent macrolide exposure raises clarithromycin-resistance concern, so bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline) is preferred.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.src: L05 S30; S33; SG U3-R7; SG U3-M
items.stem: Which antiemetic acts at H1 and muscarinic receptors from the vestibular system?
items.why: Motion sickness is vestibular — H1/M1 blockers such as meclizine and scopolamine fit.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman who may become pregnant needs NSAID ulcer prophylaxis. Which drug is inappropriate?
items.why: Misoprostol (PGE1 analog) is contraindicated in pregnancy — a potent uterotonic/abortifacient.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on warfarin and phenytoin starts an H2 blocker. Which choice raises both drug levels?
items.why: Cimetidine is a potent CYP450 inhibitor (1A2, 2C19, 3A4) that raises warfarin, phenytoin, and theophylline levels.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Two weeks after finishing H. pylori therapy, a patient still on a PPI asks for a breath test. What is the best plan?

options.B: Skip testing if symptoms are gone
options.C: Test only if an ulcer bleeds again
options.D: Test now while still on the PPI

items.why: Confirm eradication at least 4 weeks after therapy with the PPI held for 2 weeks to avoid false negatives.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 70-year-old has taken omeprazole for 8 years. Which complication is a class-wide long-term risk?
items.why: Long-term PPIs: B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, fractures, C. difficile, pneumonia, interstitial nephritis; rebound acid on stopping.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient takes omeprazole at bedtime with no benefit. What counseling best improves its effect?

options.A: Double the dose and keep bedtime timing
options.B: Take it with a calcium tablet at night
options.D: Take it 30–60 minutes before the first meal
options.E: Crush the tablet and take it with milk

items.why: PPIs work best on actively secreting pumps; dosing 30–60 minutes before the first meal matches peak pump activity.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: After 4 months of metoclopramide for gastroparesis, a patient has lip smacking. Best step?
items.why: Boxed warning: tardive dyskinesia — avoid use beyond 12 weeks.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why do PPIs suppress acid more completely than H2 receptor antagonists?

options.A: They block the pump, the final common pathway
options.B: They block both histamine and gastrin receptors
options.D: They act faster than any other class
options.E: They neutralize acid already in the stomach

items.why: Gastrin, histamine and acetylcholine converge on the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase; PPIs block it irreversibly, so suppression occurs whatever the input.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient finished H. pylori therapy last week and wants a breath test today while on a PPI. Advice?

options.E: Wait 4 weeks; hold the PPI 2 weeks

items.why: Confirm eradication at least 4 weeks after therapy, with the PPI held 2 weeks to avoid false negatives.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which adverse effect is most associated with ondansetron?
items.why: Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3; it can prolong QT; CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers may respond less.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with a new coronary stent on clopidogrel needs long-term GERD therapy. What should the clinician anticipate with omeprazole?

options.C: Less clopidogrel activation via CYP2C19 inhibition
options.D: Excess bleeding from added antiplatelet effect
options.E: No change, since both are cleared by the kidney

items.why: Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19, which activates the prodrug clopidogrel, potentially blunting its antiplatelet effect.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on bismuth quadruple therapy calls about black stools and plans to drink beer this weekend. What is the most important counseling?

options.A: Alcohol is fine; only tetracycline interacts
options.B: Black stool is expected; avoid alcohol with metronidazole
options.C: Double the PPI to stop the black stool
options.D: Take tetracycline with milk to protect the stomach
options.E: Stop all therapy — black stool means bleeding

items.why: Bismuth causes harmless black stool and tongue; metronidazole plus alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction (avoid during and 3 days after).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman who may become pregnant needs NSAID ulcer prophylaxis. Which drug is inappropriate?
items.why: Misoprostol (PGE1 analog) is contraindicated in pregnancy — a potent uterotonic/abortifacient.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient in her first trimester has persistent nausea despite diet changes. Which is typically first-line?
items.why: Pyridoxine, often combined with doxylamine, is typically first-line for nausea of pregnancy; ondansetron is used but first-trimester data are evolving.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Two weeks after finishing H. pylori therapy, a patient still on a PPI asks for a breath test. What is the best plan?

options.A: Test now while still on the PPI
options.C: Skip testing if symptoms are gone
options.E: Test only if an ulcer bleeds again

items.why: Confirm eradication at least 4 weeks after therapy with the PPI held for 2 weeks to avoid false negatives.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient takes omeprazole at bedtime and still has daytime heartburn. Best counseling?

options.B: Take it only when pain starts
options.E: Take it with antacids at night

items.why: PPIs block only actively secreting pumps; take them before the first meal so the drug peaks as pumps switch on.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with diabetic gastroparesis has taken metoclopramide for a year. What is the major safety concern?
items.why: Metoclopramide’s boxed warning is tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use or high doses — avoid beyond 12 weeks.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why can omeprazole reduce clopidogrel’s antiplatelet effect?

options.A: It binds clopidogrel in the gut

items.why: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19; omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit it. Pantoprazole has fewer CYP interactions.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with H. pylori has a penicillin allergy and took azithromycin last year. Best regimen?
items.why: Penicillin allergy rules out amoxicillin; prior macrolide exposure raises clarithromycin-resistance concern.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on sucralfate also takes levothyroxine and ciprofloxacin. Best counseling?
items.why: Sucralfate needs acid, is taken on an empty stomach, and is separated from antacids/PPIs and other drugs by 2 hours.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on warfarin and phenytoin needs an H2 blocker. Which one should be avoided?
items.why: Cimetidine is a potent CYP inhibitor (1A2, 2C19, 3A4) and raises warfarin, phenytoin, theophylline.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why should sucralfate be given on an empty stomach and apart from antacids or PPIs?

options.C: It needs acid to bind the ulcer
options.E: It irreversibly blocks the proton pump

items.why: Sucralfate polymerizes in acid (pH below 4) to form a protective barrier over the ulcer base; separate it from other drugs by 2 hours.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.src: L05 S30; S33; SG U3-R7; SG U3-M
items.stem: Which antiemetic acts at H1 and muscarinic receptors from the vestibular system?
items.why: Motion sickness is vestibular — H1/M1 blockers such as meclizine and scopolamine fit.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on warfarin and phenytoin starts an H2 blocker. Which choice raises both drug levels?
items.why: Cimetidine is a potent CYP450 inhibitor (1A2, 2C19, 3A4) that raises warfarin, phenytoin, and theophylline levels.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient beginning highly emetogenic chemotherapy needs prevention. Which regimen follows the taught principle?
items.why: Combine classes with different targets (5-HT3, NK1, dexamethasone); avoid duplicating one mechanism.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 28-year-old on daily naproxen for arthritis may become pregnant. Which ulcer-prevention drug is contraindicated?
items.why: Misoprostol, a PGE1 analog used to prevent NSAID ulcers, is contraindicated in pregnancy — a potent uterotonic/abortifacient (boxed warning).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with confirmed H. pylori took azithromycin for bronchitis 2 months ago and has no drug allergies. Which regimen is preferred?
items.why: Recent macrolide exposure raises clarithromycin-resistance concern, so bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline) is preferred.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: An older woman on a PPI for 8 years has a fragility fracture and low magnesium. Best next step?

options.E: Reassess the need for the PPI

items.why: Long-term PPI risks include fractures, hypomagnesemia, B12 deficiency, C. difficile and pneumonia — reassess periodically.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which receptor does ondansetron block?
items.why: Ondansetron blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors on gut vagal afferents and the CTZ.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on metronidazole-containing H. pylori therapy asks about drinking at a wedding. Advice?
items.why: Metronidazole causes a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which factor tips the mucosal balance toward injury by removing prostaglandin protection?
items.why: NSAIDs block COX-1 prostaglandins that drive mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow, tipping the balance toward aggression.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 19-year-old receives IV metoclopramide in the ED for vomiting. Two hours later her neck twists to one side and her eyes deviate upward. What is happening and what treats it?

options.A: Tardive dyskinesia; stop and wait months
options.C: Acute dystonia; give diphenhydramine or benztropine

items.why: D2 blockade by metoclopramide (and prochlorperazine) can cause acute dystonia within hours to days; diphenhydramine or benztropine reverses it. Tardive dyskinesia is the long-term boxed warning.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with stage 4 CKD has taken Milk of Magnesia daily for months for heartburn and constipation. She now has hypotension, absent deep-tendon reflexes and slow breathing. What is the most likely cause?

options.B: Hypermagnesemia from magnesium accumulating in CKD

items.why: Magnesium is renally cleared. In severe renal impairment it accumulates: hypotension, absent reflexes, respiratory depression and cardiac arrest. Severe renal impairment is a contraindication.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: An 86-year-old with Alzheimer dementia in a nursing home has nausea. Which antiemetic carries a boxed warning that applies directly to her?
items.why: Prochlorperazine (a phenothiazine D2 blocker) carries a boxed warning for dementia-related psychosis, plus dystonia, TD, NMS, QT prolongation and sedation.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 66-year-old had a coronary stent placed 2 months ago and takes clopidogrel and warfarin. He now has erosive GERD that needs daily acid suppression for 8 weeks. Which choice best fits?

options.B: Calcium carbonate 1,000 mg after each meal
options.D: Cimetidine 400 mg twice daily with meals
options.E: Pantoprazole 40 mg daily before a meal

items.why: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19, which omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit. Pantoprazole has fewer CYP interactions and still gives full PPI potency; cimetidine would also raise warfarin levels.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on simvastatin with no drug allergies and no prior macrolide use is about to start clarithromycin triple therapy for H. pylori. What should the clinician anticipate?

options.A: No interaction, since clarithromycin affects only warfarin
options.B: Lower simvastatin levels from CYP3A4 induction
options.D: Contraindicated: CYP3A4 inhibition raises the statin

items.why: Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibitor; co-use with simvastatin, lovastatin or ergotamine is contraindicated. It also prolongs QT. An inhibitor raises the victim drug's level and toxicity.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 52-year-old with diabetic gastroparesis also has a seizure disorder controlled on medication. Which statement about metoclopramide is correct for her?

options.A: Contraindicated because of the seizure disorder
options.B: It is safe at 10 mg before meals and at bedtime only
options.C: It is safe if limited to 12 weeks
options.D: It is fine if she has never had dystonia
options.E: It is preferred because it is prokinetic

items.why: Metoclopramide is contraindicated with GI obstruction/perforation/bleeding, pheochromocytoma, seizure disorder and a history of tardive dyskinesia. The 12-week limit is for TD risk.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient finished 14 days of H. pylori therapy 3 weeks ago and still takes omeprazole daily for reflux. He wants proof of cure this week. What is the best plan?

options.A: Stool antigen test now; a PPI does not matter
options.B: No test is needed if symptoms have resolved
options.C: Stop the PPI now and test in at least 2 weeks
options.D: Urea breath test this week while on the PPI

items.why: Test of cure (urea breath test or stool antigen) at least 4 weeks after therapy with the PPI held for 2 weeks. Stopping now satisfies both: 5+ weeks after therapy and 2 weeks off the PPI.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 35-year-old with congenital long QT syndrome starts highly emetogenic chemotherapy. Which antiemetic is contraindicated for her?
items.why: Ondansetron prolongs QT and can cause torsades; congenital long QT syndrome (and apomorphine co-use) are contraindications. A CINV regimen can lean on the NK1 antagonist and dexamethasone instead.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 29-year-old on a combined oral contraceptive and warfarin starts a CINV regimen with aprepitant. Which counseling is most accurate?

options.A: No interaction; aprepitant is not metabolized by CYP
options.B: Aprepitant raises the INR, so cut the warfarin dose now
options.C: Aprepitant raises the contraceptive's estrogen level
options.D: Stop warfarin for the 3 days of aprepitant
options.E: Use backup contraception and expect closer INR checks

items.why: Aprepitant is a CYP3A4 substrate and moderate inhibitor that lowers the effect of warfarin and hormonal contraceptives: use backup contraception and monitor the INR.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient starts bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, metronidazole). She also takes ferrous sulfate daily and chews calcium carbonate for heartburn. What is the most important counseling point about these extra products?

options.A: Take all of them together to simplify the schedule
options.B: Stop the PPI while taking calcium carbonate
options.C: Switch the iron to IV for the 14-day course
options.D: Space calcium and iron away from tetracycline
options.E: Expect black stools, so stop the iron until done

items.why: Tetracycline is chelated by dairy, antacids and iron, and calcium carbonate binds tetracyclines, quinolones, levothyroxine and iron. Space them (about 2 hours) so the antibiotic is absorbed.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 58-year-old with type 2 diabetes and CKD stage 3 has a duodenal ulcer. Sucralfate 1 g four times daily is considered. Which pair of concerns is most relevant to him?

options.E: Aluminum accumulation and higher blood glucose

items.why: Sucralfate contains aluminum that accumulates in CKD, can raise glucose in diabetes, can form bezoars and binds other drugs (separate by 2 hours).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 27-year-old needs daily naproxen for 3 months after an NSAID ulcer. She is sexually active and uses no contraception. Which ulcer prophylaxis plan is best?

options.A: Misoprostol 200 mcg four times daily with food
options.B: A daily PPI rather than misoprostol
options.C: Misoprostol now, then a pregnancy test monthly
options.D: Sucralfate taken with the naproxen doses
options.E: No prophylaxis, since the ulcer has healed

items.why: Misoprostol replaces the prostaglandins NSAIDs remove, but it is a potent uterotonic with a pregnancy boxed warning. With possible pregnancy and no contraception, a PPI protects without that risk.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A cruise passenger applied a scopolamine patch behind her ear the night before. The next day one pupil is widely dilated, but she has no headache, weakness or confusion. What is the most likely explanation?

options.B: Patch residue on her fingers touched the eye
options.D: Withdrawal from removing the patch too soon
options.E: Expected systemic effect of the patch

items.why: Scopolamine is anticholinergic; touching the patch then the eye dilates that pupil. Counsel: wash hands after handling; apply at least 4 hours before travel, replace every 72 hours; avoid in narrow-angle glaucoma.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.src: L05 S23; S25; S61; SG U3-R6; SG U3-S
items.stem: A patient with confirmed H. pylori has a penicillin allergy, took azithromycin 3 months ago and drinks 2 glasses of wine nightly. Which plan is best?

options.A: Amoxicillin triple therapy; avoid alcohol during therapy
options.B: Bismuth quadruple; no alcohol until 3 days after
options.C: PPI alone for 8 weeks, then retest
options.D: Bismuth quadruple therapy; alcohol is fine after day 7
options.E: Clarithromycin triple therapy; limit wine to one glass

items.why: Penicillin allergy or recent macrolide exposure → bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, metronidazole) for 14 days. Metronidazole causes a disulfiram-like reaction: avoid alcohol during and for 3 days after.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: An 84-year-old with a creatinine clearance of 28 mL/min takes famotidine 40 mg twice daily. Over a week she becomes confused and agitated. Infection workup is negative. What is the most likely explanation and fix?

options.A: Renal accumulation; lower the famotidine dose
options.B: Hypomagnesemia from H2 blockade; add magnesium hydroxide
options.C: Tolerance to famotidine; double the dose
options.D: Cimetidine-like CYP inhibition; switch to omeprazole

items.why: Famotidine is renally cleared: reduce the dose when CrCl is below 60 mL/min. Accumulation in CKD causes CNS effects, especially in older adults — a Unit 1 renal-dosing principle applied to a Unit 3 drug.

items.text: Why is atropine in Lomotil? At the tiny dose given it does nothing — but anyone taking big doses to get high gets unpleasant anticholinergic effects.

items.text: Biologic agents share both their targeted mechanisms and their immunosuppression-related safety profile across organ systems (RA in Lecture 2, IBD here).

items.label: High-yield
items.text: TPMT/NUDT15 before thiopurines; allopurinol → cut dose by 2/3–3/4.
items.cloze: TPMT/NUDT15 before thiopurines; allopurinol → {{c1::cut dose by 2/3–3/4}}.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why is vedolizumab gut-selective? α4β7 integrin is the gut-homing address tag; block it and leukocytes can’t enter the bowel, while immunity elsewhere is spared.
items.back: α4β7 integrin is the gut-homing address tag; block it and leukocytes can’t enter the bowel, while immunity elsewhere is spared.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why give folic acid with sulfasalazine? Sulfapyridine causes folate deficiency.
items.front: Why give folic acid with sulfasalazine?

items.label: How it works
items.text: 1. Acid-peptic disease and antiemetics are managed by targeting specific points along well-defined pathways (parietal cell secretion; the vomiting reflex).
items.cloze: {{c1::1}}. Acid-peptic disease and antiemetics are managed by targeting specific points along well-defined pathways (parietal cell secretion; the vomiting reflex).

items.label: How it works
items.text: 2. PPIs are the most potent antisecretory agents, but long-term use carries real risks that warrant periodic reassessment.
items.cloze: {{c1::2}}. PPIs are the most potent antisecretory agents, but long-term use carries real risks that warrant periodic reassessment.

items.label: How it works
items.text: 3. IBD therapy follows a step-wise escalation matched to disease severity. 4. Biologic agents share mechanisms and immunosuppression risk across organ systems. 5. Nutrition and supplements are not inert.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why do PPIs provide more complete acid suppression than H2 receptor antagonists?

options.A: They block only the gastrin pathway
options.B: They block the final common pathway (the proton pump) regardless of upstream signal
options.C: They neutralize acid directly, like antacids

items.why: PPIs block the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump itself — the final common pathway for gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine signals — unlike H2RAs, which block only the histamine input.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient recently exposed to a macrolide antibiotic needs H. pylori eradication. Which regimen best avoids the concern this history raises?
items.why: Recent macrolide exposure raises concern for clarithromycin resistance, favoring bismuth quadruple therapy over standard clarithromycin-based triple therapy.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which pairing correctly matches an antiemetic with its receptor target?
items.why: Aprepitant blocks the NK1 receptor. Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3; meclizine blocks H1/M1; metoclopramide blocks D2.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with suspected C. difficile infection asks for something to stop their diarrhea. What is the main concern with giving loperamide here?

options.B: Slowing transit can worsen toxin-mediated colonic injury
options.D: There is no concern in this scenario

items.why: Antimotility agents can worsen outcomes in infectious/inflammatory diarrhea like C. difficile by delaying clearance of toxin and slowing transit, raising risk of complications such as toxic megacolon.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which IBD agent is most gut-selective in its mechanism, rather than broadly systemically immunosuppressive?
items.why: Vedolizumab blocks α4β7 integrin-mediated leukocyte gut-homing, giving it a more gut-selective mechanism than TNF-α inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, or thiopurine immunomodulators.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A warfarin patient’s INR drops after starting St. John’s Wort. What mechanism explains this?
items.why: St. John’s Wort is a CYP3A4 inducer, increasing warfarin metabolism and lowering its anticoagulant effect (and INR) — a pharmacokinetic drug-herb interaction.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Rank the laxative classes by onset, fastest first.

options.D: All laxative classes act within the same hour
options.E: Stool softener, then bulk-forming, then stimulant

items.why: Osmotic and stimulant act within hours; bulk-forming and stool softeners take about 2–2.5 days (S6; SG U3-R9).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why does diphenoxylate/atropine contain a subtherapeutic dose of atropine?

options.A: To speed peristalsis and balance constipation
options.B: To block mu receptors in the brain
options.C: To increase P-gp efflux from the CNS

items.why: Atropine is included at a subtherapeutic dose specifically to discourage misuse/overdose (S7; SG U3-R10).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which laxative works by activating guanylate cyclase-C to increase intestinal fluid secretion?
items.why: Linaclotide is a guanylate cyclase-C agonist secretagogue (S47; S5).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient needs relief from constipation tonight before a trip. Which class fits worst?
items.why: Bulk-forming agents take the longest; a patient who needs relief tonight is not a bulk-forming candidate (S6 notes).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A Crohn patient on azathioprine develops gout and is started on allopurinol. What must happen?

options.A: Cut the azathioprine dose by two-thirds to three-quarters
options.B: No change — they use different enzymes
options.D: Stop azathioprine and start prednisone long term
options.E: Double the azathioprine to keep remission

items.why: Allopurinol blocks thiopurine metabolism; reduce the thiopurine dose by about two-thirds to three-quarters (S15).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why is budesonide associated with fewer systemic steroid effects than prednisone?

options.A: It is a 5-ASA prodrug cleaved in the colon
options.B: It blocks α4β7 integrin in the gut
options.C: It has no glucocorticoid activity at all
options.D: High first-pass metabolism limits systemic exposure
options.E: It is taken once monthly by injection

items.why: Budesonide has high first-pass metabolism — less systemic exposure than prednisone (S14).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Before starting infliximab for Crohn disease, which steps are required?

options.A: TPMT and NUDT15 genotyping only, nothing else
options.B: A baseline DEXA scan of the spine only
options.C: TB, hepatitis B/C screening; vaccines first
options.D: G6PD activity testing before the infusion
options.E: Nothing until an infection actually appears

items.why: Screen for tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C, and update vaccines (especially live) before starting biologics (S18).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why are fat-soluble vitamins more prone to toxicity than water-soluble vitamins?

options.A: They are excreted renally and build up in CKD
options.B: They are stored in fat and liver and accumulate
options.D: They are absorbed without fat or bile

items.why: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored and accumulate; water-soluble vitamins are renally excreted and rarely toxic (S22; SG U3-R12).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A severely malnourished patient is about to start feeding. Which plan prevents refeeding syndrome?

options.B: Start at full calories to correct deficits fast
options.C: Start slowly, give thiamine, check phosphate/K/Mg daily
options.E: Use parenteral nutrition even though the gut works

items.why: Start feeding slowly, give thiamine before feeding, and check phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily at first (S29).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: How do long-term PPIs cause B12 deficiency?

options.A: They block ileal uptake like metformin
options.B: They speed renal excretion of B12
options.C: They bind B12 in the gut like antacids
options.D: They destroy intrinsic factor in the ileum
options.E: Less acid frees less B12 from food protein

items.why: Stomach acid and pepsin release B12 from food protein; PPIs reduce acid (S25; SG U3-R12).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on warfarin asks whether to stop eating leafy greens. What is the right counseling?

options.A: Double greens on days INR is low
options.B: Take ginkgo to balance the greens
options.C: Diet never affects warfarin at all
options.E: Avoid all vitamin K foods completely

items.why: Keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than avoiding it; check INR when starting or stopping supplements (S27).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on warfarin starts glucosamine for knee arthritis. What does the textbook warn?

options.A: The INR may rise, increasing bleeding risk
options.C: No interaction — glucosamine is a food
options.D: The INR will fall from CYP3A4 induction
options.E: Glucosamine supplies vitamin K and lowers INR

items.why: Glucosamine sulfate may increase the INR in patients taking warfarin; avoid or monitor carefully (p. 1216).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on an SSRI starts St. John’s wort for mood. What risk should be flagged?
items.why: St. John’s wort adds serotonin syndrome risk with antidepressants and induces CYP3A4 (lowers many drug levels).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: How does lubiprostone relieve constipation?
items.why: Lubiprostone activates ClC-2 → more chloride and fluid secretion; nausea is classic.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why are thiopurines not used to treat an acute IBD flare?
items.why: Azathioprine/6-MP are maintenance drugs with slow onset; steroids induce remission during flares.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with CKD stage 4 has chronic constipation. Which laxative should be avoided?
items.why: Magnesium laxatives need caution in CKD — magnesium accumulates.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with moderate-to-severe Crohn disease is about to start infliximab. Which pre-treatment step is required?

options.E: Give a live vaccine after the first dose

items.why: Before biologics: TB and hepatitis B/C screening, vaccines (especially live) updated first, then regular labs.

items.why: Keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than avoiding it; INR is dosed against usual intake.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Three days after clindamycin, a patient has profuse watery diarrhea and fever. Which plan is correct?
items.why: This is concerning for C. difficile; avoid antimotility agents and treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on long-term metformin and a PPI has numb feet and macrocytic anemia. What should be checked?
items.why: Long-term PPI and metformin use impair B12 (less acid release; impaired ileal uptake); deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with G6PD deficiency and ulcerative colitis needs a 5-ASA drug. Which should be avoided?
items.why: Sulfasalazine’s sulfapyridine causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, rash, agranulocytosis and folate deficiency.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which vitamins carry the greatest accumulation and toxicity risk?
items.why: Fat-soluble vitamins are stored in fat and liver and accumulate; water-soluble vitamins are renally excreted and rarely toxic.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why are thiopurines not used to treat an acute IBD flare?
items.why: Azathioprine/6-MP are maintenance drugs with slow onset; steroids induce remission during flares.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A warfarin patient asks whether to stop eating leafy greens. What is the best counseling?
items.why: Keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than avoiding it; INR is dosed against usual intake.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient takes very large doses of loperamide to get high. What toxicity is the main concern?
items.why: Very high loperamide doses cause QT prolongation, torsades and cardiac arrest; naloxone reverses CNS depression.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A Crohn patient on azathioprine is prescribed allopurinol for gout. What must happen?

options.E: Switch to febuxostat with no change

items.why: Allopurinol blocks thiopurine metabolism; reduce the thiopurine dose by about two-thirds to three-quarters (febuxostat avoided).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on apixaban asks about ginkgo for memory. What is the key concern?
items.why: Ginkgo (and fish oil) can increase bleeding risk, especially with anticoagulants/antiplatelets; stop before surgery.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with CKD stage 4 has chronic constipation. Which laxative should be avoided?
items.why: Magnesium laxatives need caution in CKD — magnesium accumulates.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why is budesonide associated with fewer systemic effects than prednisone?
items.why: Budesonide is extensively metabolized on first pass, so less reaches the systemic circulation.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient stable on warfarin starts St. John’s wort for mood. What should the clinician anticipate?

options.A: No change, since it is natural
options.C: Higher INR from added vitamin K

items.why: St. John’s wort induces CYP3A4, speeding warfarin metabolism and lowering INR; check INR when starting or stopping any supplement.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Three days after clindamycin, a patient has profuse watery diarrhea and fever. Which plan is correct?
items.why: This is concerning for C. difficile; avoid antimotility agents and treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with newly diagnosed mild ulcerative colitis is starting therapy. Which drug fits first?
items.why: 5-ASA agents are first-line for mild-to-moderate UC with a favorable safety profile; biologics are reserved for moderate-to-severe disease.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why does refeeding a starved patient drop phosphate, potassium and magnesium?

options.A: They are lost in the stool

items.why: Carbohydrate raises insulin, which drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells — dangerous lows.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why does diphenoxylate/atropine contain a low dose of atropine?
items.why: Atropine is included at a subtherapeutic dose specifically to discourage misuse/overdose; the product is Schedule V.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Before starting azathioprine for Crohn maintenance, which test is most important?
items.why: Test TPMT and NUDT15 before thiopurines; low activity raises myelosuppression risk.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on an SSRI starts St. John’s wort for mood. What risk should be flagged?
items.why: St. John’s wort adds serotonin syndrome risk with antidepressants and induces CYP3A4 (lowers many drug levels).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on iron tablets also takes daily omeprazole and has persistent iron deficiency. Why?
items.why: Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C and impaired by antacids and PPIs.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which IBD agent is most gut-selective?
items.why: Vedolizumab blocks α4β7 integrin-mediated leukocyte gut-homing — less systemic immunosuppression.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which laxative class has the slowest onset but is generally safest for long-term use?
items.why: Bulk-forming agents absorb water and expand stool; slowest onset, safest long term; need fluids, avoid in obstruction.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A severely malnourished patient with a functional gut needs nutrition. What is the best plan?
items.why: Use the gut if it works; refeed slowly, give thiamine before feeding, and check phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily at the start.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: How does lubiprostone relieve constipation?
items.why: Lubiprostone activates ClC-2 → more chloride and fluid secretion; nausea is classic.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with moderate-to-severe Crohn disease is about to start infliximab. Which pre-treatment step is required?

options.B: Give a live vaccine after the first dose

items.why: Before biologics: TB and hepatitis B/C screening, vaccines (especially live) updated first, then regular labs.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on long-term metformin and a PPI has numb feet and macrocytic anemia. What should be checked?
items.why: Long-term PPI and metformin use impair B12 (less acid release; impaired ileal uptake); deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A parent asks for diphenoxylate/atropine for a 4-year-old with watery diarrhea and no fever. What is the best answer?

options.A: Yes, at half the adult dose
options.B: Yes; the atropine prevents any overdose
options.C: Use loperamide instead at the adult dose
options.D: No: under 6 it can depress breathing

items.why: Diphenoxylate/atropine is contraindicated under 6 years (respiratory depression and anticholinergic toxicity, especially in children). The atropine is a subtherapeutic dose to deter misuse.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Before azathioprine is started for Crohn disease, genetic testing shows very low TPMT activity. What should the clinician anticipate?

options.A: High myelosuppression risk at standard doses
options.B: Faster onset of remission within days
options.C: No change, since TPMT affects only allopurinol
options.D: Lower drug levels, so a higher dose is needed
options.E: Higher risk of acute pancreatitis only

items.why: Test TPMT and NUDT15 before thiopurines: low activity raises myelosuppression risk. Monitor CBC and liver tests; onset takes weeks to months — a Unit 1 pharmacogenomics principle.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with mild ulcerative colitis has taken mesalamine 4.8 g daily for 6 months. His creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.6 mg/dL with no other cause. What is the most likely explanation?
items.why: Mesalamine (5-ASA) is first-line for mild UC; its key toxicity is interstitial nephritis, so creatinine is monitored. Acute intolerance syndrome mimics a flare.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.src: L06 S4; S5; S47; SG U3-R9
items.stem: A grandmother asks if she can give her 18-month-old grandson some of her linaclotide for constipation. What is the key safety point?

options.A: Boxed warning: fatal dehydration under age 2
options.B: It is safe if mixed with plenty of fluid
options.C: It is safe at one quarter of the adult capsule dose
options.D: It only causes mild diarrhea in children
options.E: It is safe because it is not absorbed

items.why: Linaclotide (a secretagogue) has a boxed warning against use in children under 2 years — severe dehydration and deaths; also mechanical GI obstruction is a contraindication.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 70-year-old on metformin and long-term omeprazole has macrocytic anemia. Folic acid alone is started; the anemia improves, but numbness in her feet worsens. What happened?

options.C: B12 deficiency masked by the folate

items.why: PPIs and metformin impair B12 absorption. Folate alone can correct the anemia while neurologic damage from B12 deficiency progresses and can become irreversible. Check and replace B12.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with Crohn disease in remission on azathioprine now has recurrent gout and needs urate-lowering therapy. Which plan is safest?

options.A: Stop azathioprine permanently before any gout drug
options.B: Febuxostat at the usual starting dose
options.C: Add colchicine daily instead of urate-lowering therapy
options.D: Allopurinol plus a major azathioprine dose cut
options.E: Allopurinol at full dose with no azathioprine change

items.why: Xanthine oxidase metabolizes thiopurines. Allopurinol requires a major thiopurine dose cut (about two-thirds to three-quarters) with CBC monitoring; febuxostat use with azathioprine is contraindicated.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: An 81-year-old with an esophageal stricture and trouble swallowing has chronic constipation. Which option is the best fit?

options.B: Psyllium 3.4 g with a full glass of water
options.E: Polyethylene glycol 3350, 17 g in fluid daily

items.why: Bulk-forming laxatives (psyllium, methylcellulose) can obstruct the esophagus or intestine without enough fluid and are contraindicated with dysphagia. PEG 3350 is an osmotic agent mixed into fluid.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with Crohn disease takes budesonide 9 mg every morning. He starts ketoconazole for a fungal infection and drinks grapefruit juice daily. Two weeks later he has a round face and high glucose. Why?

options.A: CYP3A4 inhibition raised budesonide's systemic exposure
options.E: Expected effect of 9 mg on any regimen

items.why: Budesonide's high first-pass metabolism (CYP3A4) keeps systemic exposure low. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, grapefruit juice) remove that protection → hypercortisolism.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient starting sulfasalazine for ulcerative colitis has G6PD deficiency and a sulfa allergy. What is the best decision?

options.A: Use sulfasalazine with folic acid 1 mg daily
options.C: Use sulfasalazine and check a CBC monthly
options.D: Skip 5-ASA therapy and start a biologic
options.E: Use sulfasalazine at half the usual dose

items.why: Sulfasalazine is contraindicated with sulfa or salicylate allergy and causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency (plus agranulocytosis, SJS, folate deficiency). Mesalamine delivers 5-ASA without the sulfa component.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on warfarin has had stable INRs of 2.5 for a year. Over 3 weeks her INR falls to 1.4 with perfect adherence. She recently started a mood supplement. Which mechanism best explains this?

options.B: Vitamin K deficiency from the supplement
options.D: Ginkgo biloba increased clotting factor synthesis

items.why: St. John's wort induces CYP3A4, increasing warfarin metabolism and lowering the INR. That is why supplement use is a required part of medication reconciliation.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with cirrhosis takes lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy. He now has 8 watery stools a day, is dizzy, and his sodium is high. What is the best adjustment?

options.A: Keep the dose and add magnesium hydroxide
options.B: Increase lactulose to clear more ammonia
options.C: Reduce it to reach 2–3 soft stools a day
options.E: Switch to senna for gentler stools

items.why: Lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy is titrated to 2–3 soft stools a day; over-use causes dehydration and hypernatremia.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A severely malnourished patient who has barely eaten for 3 weeks is about to start nutrition support. Which plan best prevents refeeding syndrome?

options.A: Give thiamine only after feeding begins
options.B: Check electrolytes weekly once feeding starts
options.C: Start full calories at once to restore weight quickly
options.D: Use IV glucose alone for the first 3 days
options.E: Thiamine first, slow start, daily phosphate/K/Mg

items.why: Carbohydrate feeding raises insulin, shifting phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells — dangerously low levels with heart, muscle and breathing problems. Feed slowly, monitor daily, give thiamine first.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 62-year-old smoker with ulcerative colitis and a prior myocardial infarction has failed infliximab. Tofacitinib is proposed. Which concern weighs most heavily?

options.B: Tardive dyskinesia with use beyond 12 weeks
options.C: Boxed warnings for MACE and thrombosis

items.why: Tofacitinib (JAK inhibitor) carries boxed warnings for serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and thrombosis — highest stakes in an older smoker with prior MI. It is used after TNF-inhibitor failure.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Four days after finishing clindamycin for a dental abscess, a patient has profuse watery diarrhea and a fever of 38.6 °C. He asks for loperamide. What is the best response?

options.A: Start bismuth subsalicylate and recheck in a week
options.B: Give loperamide 4 mg, then 2 mg after each stool
options.D: Avoid it; evaluate for C. difficile first

items.why: Recent antibiotics + fever + profuse watery diarrhea suggests C. difficile; antimotility agents (loperamide, diphenoxylate) are avoided because slowing transit can worsen toxin-mediated injury. Treat the cause.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 31-year-old in opioid withdrawal has been taking 40 mg of OTC loperamide daily to ease symptoms. He presents with syncope. What is the most important next step?

options.A: Check a stool culture for infection
options.B: Get an ECG for QT prolongation and arrhythmia
options.C: Reassure: loperamide does not reach the brain
options.D: Switch to diphenoxylate/atropine at the same dose
options.E: Give naloxone and discharge if he wakes

items.why: Loperamide maximum is 16 mg/day Rx (8 mg OTC). High doses cause QT prolongation, torsades and cardiac arrest; CNS depression in overdose may need repeated naloxone.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with acromegaly starts pegvisomant. Which lab best tracks the response?
items.why: Pegvisomant blocks the GH receptor so IGF-1 falls; GH rises and is not used to monitor it (S7).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: How does cabergoline treat a prolactinoma?
items.why: Dopamine normally inhibits prolactin; D2 agonists restore that tone and often shrink the tumor (S8–S9; SG U4-R3).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: How do octreotide and lanreotide treat acromegaly?
items.why: Somatostatin analogs bind somatostatin receptors and suppress GH release (S6–S7).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with central diabetes insipidus starts desmopressin. What is the main safety counseling?
items.why: Desmopressin keeps free water; risk is hyponatremia — monitor sodium and limit fluids (S10).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with SIADH stays hyponatremic despite fluid restriction. Tolvaptan is planned. Why start it in hospital?

options.B: It must be given IV only

items.why: Tolvaptan can overcorrect sodium (osmotic demyelination) and injure the liver; start in hospital (S10).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A woman taking levothyroxine with her calcium and iron each morning has a high TSH. Best advice?

options.A: Separate them by at least 4 hours

items.why: Calcium, iron and antacids reduce absorption — separate by at least 4 hours; take it 30–60 minutes before breakfast (S12–S13).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A woman in her first trimester has hyperthyroidism. Which drug is preferred?
items.why: PTU is preferred in the first trimester; methimazole is avoided then (teratogenic) (S15).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Six weeks into methimazole, a patient has fever and a sore throat. What should happen?

options.E: Stop it and check a CBC

items.why: Thionamides carry an agranulocytosis warning; fever or sore throat → stop and check a CBC (S15).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why is PTU preferred over methimazole in thyroid storm?
items.why: PTU blocks synthesis and conversion, a faster effect on active hormone (S14–S15).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: What is levothyroxine, and how does it act?
items.why: Levothyroxine is synthetic T4, converted peripherally to active T3, which binds nuclear receptors (S12–S13).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: An 80-year-old with coronary disease is newly hypothyroid. How should levothyroxine be started?

options.A: A loading dose then full dose

items.why: Older adults and cardiac patients start low and titrate slowly to avoid angina or arrhythmia (S12).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A hypothyroid woman on levothyroxine learns she is pregnant. What dose change does the textbook advise?
items.why: Many pregnant hypothyroid patients need about 25–30% more thyroxine; add two extra doses a week as soon as pregnancy is confirmed (p. 734).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why must chronic glucocorticoid therapy be tapered rather than stopped?

options.C: The suppressed HPA axis needs time to recover
options.D: Because the adrenal gland is destroyed

items.why: Exogenous steroid suppresses CRH and ACTH; abrupt withdrawal leaves too little endogenous cortisol (S22; SG U4-R8).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with primary adrenal insufficiency is on hydrocortisone but has low BP and high potassium. What should be added?
items.why: Addison disease needs mineralocorticoid replacement alongside a glucocorticoid (S20).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: What does fludrocortisone do at the kidney?
items.why: Mineralocorticoids promote renal sodium retention and potassium excretion; monitor BP and potassium (S20).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: How do chronic exogenous glucocorticoids cause adrenal insufficiency on abrupt withdrawal?

options.E: They raise ACTH until it is exhausted

items.why: Chronic steroid suppresses CRH/ACTH via negative feedback, so endogenous cortisol cannot resume quickly (S22; S28).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which drug lowers cortisol by blocking 11-β-hydroxylase?
items.why: Metyrapone blocks the final step of cortisol synthesis (S23–S24).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with Cushing syndrome on mifepristone has persistently high cortisol levels. What explains this?

options.E: It increases ACTH secretion by itself

items.why: Mifepristone blocks the glucocorticoid receptor, so cortisol levels rise — monitor clinically (S24).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which pairing of drug and mechanism in Cushing syndrome is correct?
items.why: Ketoconazole blocks several steroidogenic CYPs; metyrapone the last cortisol step; mifepristone the glucocorticoid receptor; spironolactone the mineralocorticoid receptor.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient’s levothyroxine dose was changed today. When should TSH be rechecked?
items.why: T4’s 7-day half-life means steady state takes about 6 weeks; recheck TSH at 6–8 weeks.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman with galactorrhea and amenorrhea has a prolactinoma. First-line therapy?
items.why: Dopamine agonists restore dopamine’s inhibitory brake on prolactin; cabergoline is twice weekly and better tolerated.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with Addison disease on hydrocortisone has low BP and high potassium. What should be added?
items.why: Primary adrenal insufficiency needs mineralocorticoid replacement alongside a glucocorticoid.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease on high-dose cabergoline needs monitoring for which serious effect?
items.why: High-dose cabergoline (Parkinson doses) is linked to valvulopathy; lower prolactinoma doses carry less risk.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Five weeks into methimazole, a patient has fever and a sore throat. What should happen?

options.A: Stop it and check a CBC

items.why: Thionamides carry an agranulocytosis boxed warning; fever or sore throat → stop and check a CBC.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with Graves disease is in thyroid storm and on long-term prednisone. What extra role do steroids play?

options.C: They have no role in storm

items.why: Corticosteroids blunt peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion and cover relative adrenal insufficiency.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with SIADH stays hyponatremic despite fluid restriction. Tolvaptan is chosen. Key safety step?

options.C: Give with salt tablets at home

items.why: Tolvaptan can overcorrect sodium (osmotic demyelination) and injure the liver — start in hospital.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient’s levothyroxine dose was changed today. When should TSH be rechecked?
items.why: T4’s 7-day half-life means steady state takes about 6 weeks; recheck TSH at 6–8 weeks.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient starting desmopressin for central diabetes insipidus asks what to watch for. Best counseling?
items.why: Desmopressin keeps free water; the risk is hyponatremia — monitor sodium and limit fluids.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with untreated Graves disease arrives febrile, tachycardic and confused. Correct sequence?
items.why: Iodine is given only after PTU; giving it first supplies substrate for new synthesis before synthesis is blocked.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on octreotide for acromegaly develops right-upper-quadrant pain after meals. Most likely cause?
items.why: Octreotide/lanreotide: GI upset, gallstones and bradycardia.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which pairing of drug and mechanism in Cushing syndrome is correct?
items.why: Ketoconazole blocks several steroidogenic CYPs; metyrapone the last cortisol step; mifepristone the glucocorticoid receptor; spironolactone the mineralocorticoid receptor.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why is PTU preferred over methimazole in thyroid storm?
items.why: PTU blocks synthesis and peripheral conversion — a faster effect on active hormone.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on chronic prednisone ran out of refills; now hypotensive, weak and confused. Best management?
items.why: Adrenal crisis from abrupt withdrawal after HPA suppression — immediate IV hydrocortisone and fluids.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease on high-dose cabergoline needs monitoring for which serious effect?
items.why: High-dose cabergoline (Parkinson doses) is linked to valvulopathy; lower prolactinoma doses carry less risk.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Five weeks into methimazole, a patient has fever and a sore throat. What should happen?

options.B: Stop it and check a CBC

items.why: Thionamides carry an agranulocytosis boxed warning; fever or sore throat → stop and check a CBC.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient starting a 3-month prednisone course asks how to take it. Best counseling?

options.A: Double doses if you miss one
options.B: At bedtime on an empty stomach

items.why: Take in the morning with food; consider bone and GI protection; taper chronic therapy.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why does long-term exogenous hormone therapy suppress the gland above it?
items.why: The peripheral hormone feeds back on the hypothalamus/pituitary, turning the levels above it down.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: An 82-year-old with coronary artery disease is newly hypothyroid. How should levothyroxine start?
items.why: Older adults and cardiac patients start low and titrate slowly to avoid angina or arrhythmia.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on amiodarone develops thyroid dysfunction. What should be expected after stopping it?
items.why: Amiodarone can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism; it persists after stopping because of its very long half-life.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with SIADH stays hyponatremic despite fluid restriction. Tolvaptan is chosen. Key safety step?

options.A: Give with salt tablets at home

items.why: Tolvaptan can overcorrect sodium (osmotic demyelination) and injure the liver — start in hospital.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on levothyroxine starts an oral contraceptive. What change should be anticipated?
items.why: Estrogens raise thyroid-binding globulin, so levothyroxine needs rise — check TSH.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with acromegaly is started on pegvisomant. Which lab tracks the response?
items.why: Pegvisomant blocks the GH receptor so IGF-1 falls; GH rises and is not used to monitor it.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with Cushing syndrome on ketoconazole starts simvastatin. What is the concern?
items.why: Ketoconazole: hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation and strong CYP3A4 inhibition.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with Addison disease on hydrocortisone has low BP and high potassium. What should be added?
items.why: Primary adrenal insufficiency needs mineralocorticoid replacement alongside a glucocorticoid.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman on levothyroxine takes it with her calcium and iron at breakfast; her TSH is high. Best advice?
items.why: Calcium, iron and antacids reduce absorption; take levothyroxine 30–60 minutes before breakfast, 4 hours apart.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on haloperidol develops galactorrhea and a high prolactin. What explains it?
items.why: Antipsychotics and metoclopramide raise prolactin by blocking dopamine’s inhibitory brake.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with asthma is in thyroid storm. Which drug choice needs caution?
items.why: Propranolol is avoided in asthma and decompensated heart failure; it blunts symptoms and conversion.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which glucocorticoid is the most potent relative to hydrocortisone?
items.why: Potency vs. hydrocortisone: prednisone about 4×, dexamethasone about 25–30×.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman with galactorrhea and amenorrhea has a prolactinoma. First-line therapy?
items.why: Dopamine agonists restore dopamine’s inhibitory brake on prolactin; cabergoline is twice weekly and better tolerated.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with Graves disease is in thyroid storm and on long-term prednisone. What extra role do steroids play?

options.E: They have no role in storm

items.why: Corticosteroids blunt peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion and cover relative adrenal insufficiency.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on spironolactone for hyperaldosteronism also takes lisinopril. What should be monitored?
items.why: Spironolactone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor; ACEi/ARBs and potassium add to hyperkalemia.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman at 9 weeks’ gestation has Graves hyperthyroidism. Which drug is preferred now?
items.why: PTU is preferred in the first trimester (methimazole teratogenic); switch to methimazole after.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Choosing the most potent glucose-lowering drug instead of the safest for an older adult who falls.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Integrated case — diabetes: a DPP-4 or SGLT2 inhibitor is preferable to a sulfonylurea given the fall history — sulfonylureas force glucose-independent insulin release, raising hypoglycemia-driven fall risk.
items.back: a DPP-4 or SGLT2 inhibitor is preferable to a sulfonylurea given the fall history — sulfonylureas force glucose-independent insulin release, raising hypoglycemia-driven fall risk.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Integrated case — thyroid storm: beta-blocker + PTU first, then iodine solution only after PTU (never before — iodine first would supply substrate for new hormone synthesis before synthesis is blocked, worsening the crisis).
items.back: beta-blocker + PTU first, then iodine solution only after PTU (never before — iodine first would supply substrate for new hormone synthesis before synthesis is blocked, worsening the crisis).

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Corticosteroids also help in thyroid storm by blunting peripheral conversion and covering relative adrenal insufficiency.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Shared concept: effective endocrine drug selection depends on knowing exactly where in a pathway (or which receptor/site) a drug acts — that position determines both its efficacy and its specific risks.
items.back: effective endocrine drug selection depends on knowing exactly where in a pathway (or which receptor/site) a drug acts — that position determines both its efficacy and its specific risks.

items.label: How it works
items.text: 1. The hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland axis is a shared template across thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal pharmacology — exogenous hormone therapy suppresses the levels above it via negative feedback.
items.cloze: {{c1::1}}. The hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland axis is a shared template across thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal pharmacology — exogenous hormone therapy suppresses the levels above it via negative feedback.

items.label: How it works
items.text: 2. Antithyroid drug selection (methimazole vs. PTU) and glucocorticoid tapering both hinge on understanding exactly where and how each drug intervenes in its pathway.
items.cloze: {{c1::2}}. Antithyroid drug selection (methimazole vs. PTU) and glucocorticoid tapering both hinge on understanding exactly where and how each drug intervenes in its pathway.

items.label: How it works
items.text: 3. Glucose-lowering drugs act at distinct sites (pancreas, liver, muscle/fat, kidney, gut, incretin axis) — drug selection balances efficacy against hypoglycemia and other class-specific risks.
items.cloze: {{c1::3}}. Glucose-lowering drugs act at distinct sites (pancreas, liver, muscle/fat, kidney, gut, incretin axis) — drug selection balances efficacy against hypoglycemia and other class-specific risks.

items.label: How it works
items.text: 4. Hyperparathyroidism and hypoparathyroidism require opposite drug strategies (lowering vs. raising effective PTH activity) — a new angle distinct from, but related to, the osteoporosis pharmacotherapy of Unit 2.
items.cloze: {{c1::4}}. Hyperparathyroidism and hypoparathyroidism require opposite drug strategies (lowering vs. raising effective PTH activity) — a new angle distinct from, but related to, the osteoporosis pharmacotherapy of Unit 2.

items.label: How it works
items.text: 5. Endocrine pharmacology is deeply interconnected — spironolactone, dopamine agonists, and SERMs each reappear across more than one organ system in this unit alone.
items.back: spironolactone, dopamine agonists, and SERMs each reappear across more than one organ system in this unit alone.
items.cloze: {{c1::5}}. Endocrine pharmacology is deeply interconnected — spironolactone, dopamine agonists, and SERMs each reappear across more than one organ system in this unit alone.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Connecting back: osteoporosis pharmacology (Unit 2) and drug-metabolism/interaction concepts (Unit 1) both reappear here — pharmacology is cumulative, not siloed by unit.
