items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why is PTU, rather than methimazole, preferred in the management of thyroid storm?

options.B: PTU additionally blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion
options.D: PTU works faster at the level of iodide trapping

items.why: PTU blocks both new thyroid hormone synthesis and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, giving it a faster effect on circulating active hormone than methimazole — important in the acute setting of thyroid storm.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on chronic glucocorticoid therapy abruptly stops the medication and develops hypotension and weakness. What is the underlying mechanism?

options.A: Direct adrenal gland destruction by the drug
options.B: HPA-axis suppression leaving endogenous cortisol production unable to resume quickly
options.C: An allergic reaction to the glucocorticoid

items.why: Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid exposure suppresses CRH/ACTH via negative feedback (Figure 9), reducing the adrenal cortex’s stimulus to produce cortisol; abrupt withdrawal does not give the axis time to recover, precipitating adrenal insufficiency.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which contraceptive counseling point reflects a true contraindication to estrogen-containing combined hormonal contraception?

options.D: A family history of type 2 diabetes

items.why: Smoking at age 35 or older is a well-established contraindication to estrogen-containing contraception due to substantially increased thromboembolic and cardiovascular risk.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why do sulfonylureas carry a higher hypoglycemia risk than DPP-4 inhibitors?

options.A: Sulfonylureas force K-ATP channel closure and insulin release independent of glucose level, unlike the glucose-dependent incretin pathway
options.B: DPP-4 inhibitors have no effect on insulin secretion
options.C: Sulfonylureas work only in type 1 diabetes
options.D: There is no difference in hypoglycemia risk between these classes

items.why: Sulfonylureas bind the K-ATP channel directly and force closure regardless of glucose level (Figure 15), while incretin-based agents amplify insulin release only when glucose is already elevated — explaining the difference in hypoglycemia risk.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with hypoparathyroidism after thyroid surgery needs pharmacologic treatment. Which combination is the mainstay of therapy?
items.why: Because PTH is required to activate vitamin D, hypoparathyroidism impairs that activation step; calcitriol (already-active vitamin D) bypasses it, and is given together with oral calcium as first-line therapy.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor develops a genital yeast infection. What is the mechanistic explanation?

options.B: Increased urinary glucose excretion promoting fungal overgrowth
options.D: Systemic candidemia from the drug itself

items.why: SGLT2 inhibitors block renal glucose reabsorption, increasing urinary glucose concentration and creating a favorable environment for genital fungal overgrowth — a mechanism-based, well-known adverse effect.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A woman on a combined pill starts rifampin for latent TB. What counseling is needed?

options.B: No change; rifampin has no effect
options.E: Switch rifampin to St. John’s wort

items.why: Enzyme inducers (rifampin, some antiepileptics, St. John’s wort) lower contraceptive efficacy (S6).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which statement about tamoxifen and raloxifene is correct?
items.why: Tamoxifen is an endometrial agonist (cancer risk); raloxifene blocks the endometrium (S7–S8).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A man on finasteride for BPH has a PSA of 2.0 ng/mL. How should it be interpreted?

options.B: Stop finasteride for a month first

items.why: Finasteride lowers PSA by about half, so double the value (S9).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on insulin and propranolol has a glucose of 45 mg/dL but no tremor or palpitations. Why?

options.A: The meter is reading falsely low

items.why: Beta-blockers can mask hypoglycemia warning symptoms (S13; S67).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which insulin is the only one given intravenously?
items.why: Only regular insulin is given IV (S12 notes).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on insulin is shaky with glucose 58 mg/dL and can swallow. What first?

options.A: 1 mg glucagon IM before any carbs
options.B: 15 g fast carbs, recheck in 15 min
options.D: Give the next insulin dose early
options.E: Skip the next meal and rest

items.why: Rule of 15 (S13).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on metformin with eGFR 40 is scheduled for a CT with iodinated contrast. What should happen?

options.B: Add an SGLT2 inhibitor the same day
options.D: Hold metformin around the contrast study
options.E: Double metformin to cover the stress

items.why: Hold for contrast dye with reduced kidney function — lactic acidosis risk (S15; S67).

items.label: Self-test question

options.B: Use it with a DPP-4 inhibitor
options.D: Safe; it only affects the gut

items.why: GLP-1 RAs are contraindicated with personal or family history of MTC or MEN2 (S19).

items.why: TZDs: fluid retention/heart failure, weight gain (S14).

items.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes has NYHA class III heart failure. Which drug is contraindicated?
items.why: Thiazolidinediones cause fluid retention and are contraindicated in NYHA class III and IV heart failure (p. 799).

items.stem: What should be monitored after starting cinacalcet?
items.why: Cinacalcet lowers PTH and calcium; monitor for hypocalcemia (and QT) (S25–S26).

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why does ACE inhibitor + spironolactone raise potassium so much? Both cut aldosterone’s effect — one lowers the hormone, the other blocks its receptor — and CKD already limits K⁺ excretion.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why does a falling GFR change how a renally cleared drug must be dosed?

options.A: Absorption from the gut falls with GFR
options.B: Only the parent drug matters, not metabolites
options.C: The loading dose must always be doubled
options.D: The drug accumulates unless dose or interval is adjusted
options.E: The drug is cleared faster, so doses rise

items.why: Reduced GFR causes a renally cleared drug to accumulate if unadjusted; reduce the dose, extend the interval, or both (S5; SG U5-R1).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: An 80-year-old has pneumonia and dehydration. She takes metformin and a DOAC. What is the best dosing habit?

options.A: Stop checking renal function in older adults
options.B: Keep last year’s doses since CrCl is stable
options.C: Re-estimate CrCl now and adjust renally cleared drugs
options.D: Double the loading dose of both drugs
options.E: Adjust only the drugs with toxic metabolites

items.why: Acute illness and dehydration can drop GFR quickly; estimate CrCl or eGFR and reassess renally cleared drugs (S8).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Roughly what share of filtered sodium does each segment reabsorb, from proximal tubule to collecting duct?

options.B: About equal at 25% in every segment

items.why: Proximal tubule ~65%, thick ascending limb ~25%, distal tubule 5–8%, collecting duct 2–3% (S7 notes).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why do loop diuretics increase calcium excretion while thiazides decrease it?

options.A: Loops collapse lumen potential; thiazides aid NCX
options.B: Thiazides act on NKCC2; loops act on NCC
options.C: Loops block calcium channels; thiazides open them
options.E: Loops raise PTH; thiazides suppress PTH

items.why: Loops collapse the lumen-positive potential driving paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ reabsorption; thiazides lower cell Na⁺ so NCX reabsorbs more Ca²⁺ (S11; S13; SG U5-R3).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient has recurrent calcium kidney stones and hypertension with normal renal function. Which diuretic fits best?
items.why: Thiazides decrease calcium excretion, useful in recurrent calcium stones; first-line HTN with preserved renal function (S12; S30).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with heart failure on digoxin starts high-dose furosemide. Which lab change most raises digoxin toxicity risk?
items.why: Hypokalemia from loops increases digoxin toxicity (S38).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which adverse effect is most characteristic of loop diuretics given rapidly IV at high doses?
items.why: Ototoxicity, especially with rapid IV administration or high doses; give IV furosemide no faster than 4 mg/min (S10; S27).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: An older woman on hydrochlorothiazide is confused, with sodium 122 mEq/L. Which statement fits?

options.A: Thiazide hyponatremia, especially in older adults
options.B: Thiazides raise sodium by blocking ADH
options.D: Loop diuretics cause more hyponatremia than thiazides

items.why: Hyponatremia can be significant with thiazides, especially in older adults (S12).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with CKD on furosemide 80 mg twice daily has hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg added. Two weeks later he has lost 15 kg, BP is 91/58 and creatinine is 10.8. What happened?

options.B: Thiazide failed, so fluid built up

items.why: Adding a thiazide to chronic loop therapy can cause dramatic diuresis, hypovolemia and AKI; monitor very closely, ideally inpatient (p. 277; p. 285).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why must saline be given with furosemide to treat hypercalcemia?

options.A: Saline blocks NKCC2 with the loop
options.B: Saline prevents loop ototoxicity in the ear
options.C: Volume loss boosts proximal Ca²⁺ reabsorption

items.why: A loop alone causes volume contraction, which enhances proximal Ca²⁺ reabsorption and stops the calcium diuresis; give saline with it (p. 280).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which pairing correctly matches a potassium-sparing diuretic to its mechanism?
items.why: Amiloride and triamterene block ENaC; spironolactone and eplerenone block the mineralocorticoid receptor (S17–S18).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A man needs an aldosterone antagonist for heart failure but developed painful gynecomastia on one before. Which fits?
items.why: Spironolactone has antiandrogen effects (gynecomastia) that eplerenone largely avoids (S17; S33).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A hiker plans a rapid ascent to high altitude next week. Which diuretic is used for prophylaxis?
items.why: Acetazolamide is used for altitude sickness prophylaxis, 125–250 mg BID starting a day before ascent (S19; S36).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: How does mannitol produce diuresis?

options.A: It is filtered but not reabsorbed, holding water in the lumen
options.B: It antagonizes aldosterone at its receptor
options.C: It inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
options.D: It blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
options.E: It blocks ENaC in the collecting duct

items.why: Mannitol is an inert, filtered but poorly reabsorbed solute that holds water in the tubule lumen osmotically (S19–S20).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with decompensated heart failure and raised intracranial pressure is being considered for mannitol. What is the concern?

options.A: Mannitol is safe because it is inert
options.B: Mannitol expands ECF volume and can worsen heart failure
options.C: Mannitol has no effect on fluid status
options.D: Mannitol causes severe hyperkalemia via ENaC

items.why: Mannitol expands extracellular volume; avoid it in heart failure and volume depletion; needs intact renal perfusion (S19–S20; S37).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which acid–base change is a predictable adverse effect of acetazolamide?
items.why: Blocking carbonic anhydrase causes bicarbonate diuresis and a mild metabolic acidosis (S19–S20).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with SIADH stays hyponatremic despite fluid restriction at home. Which drug does the textbook use next?
items.why: ADH antagonists are used for SIADH when water restriction fails; tolvaptan is oral, conivaptan IV (p. 276).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: When GFR falls, which dose is usually unchanged for a renally cleared drug?
items.why: Loading doses depend on volume of distribution and are often unchanged; maintenance doses are adjusted.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A stage 3 CKD patient on lisinopril starts spironolactone; two weeks later K⁺ is 6.1 mEq/L. Best explanation?
items.why: ACE inhibitor lowers aldosterone, spironolactone blocks its receptor, and CKD limits K⁺ excretion — risk compounds.

options.B: Adjust only the antibiotics, nothing else

options.D: Double every loading dose to be safe

items.why: Reassess as renal function changes — acute illness, dehydration or nephrotoxic drugs can drop GFR quickly.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why are loop diuretics the most potent class?

options.C: They are filtered but not reabsorbed

items.why: Potency tracks the share of sodium reabsorbed at the blocked segment: loop ~25%, thiazide ~6%, CAI ~4%, K⁺-sparing ~2%.

items.label: How it works
items.text: 1. Diuretic classes (Session 1) and RAAS-blocking antihypertensives both map onto specific, drug-targetable points in renal physiology — the nephron (Figure 1) and the RAAS cascade (Figure 8), respectively.
items.cloze: {{c1::1}}. Diuretic classes (Session 1) and RAAS-blocking antihypertensives both map onto specific, drug-targetable points in renal physiology — the nephron (Figure 1) and the RAAS cascade (Figure 8), respectively.

items.label: How it works
items.text: 2. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred first-line therapy for hypertension in CKD because of their renoprotective efferent-arteriolar mechanism, not just their blood-pressure-lowering effect.
items.cloze: {{c1::2}}. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred first-line therapy for hypertension in CKD because of their renoprotective efferent-arteriolar mechanism, not just their blood-pressure-lowering effect.

items.label: How it works
items.text: 3. Calcium channel blockers exemplify the cardiovascular-renal overlap directly — the same drug class, same mechanism, treats both hypertension and angina.
items.cloze: {{c1::3}}. Calcium channel blockers exemplify the cardiovascular-renal overlap directly — the same drug class, same mechanism, treats both hypertension and angina.

items.label: How it works
items.text: 4. The "triple whammy" (NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic) is a classic, common, and preventable cause of acute kidney injury that draws on content from both sessions at once.
items.cloze: {{c1::4}}. The "triple whammy" (NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic) is a classic, common, and preventable cause of acute kidney injury that draws on content from both sessions at once.

items.label: How it works
items.text: 5. Hypertension and chronic kidney disease exist in a bidirectional, self-reinforcing cycle (Figure 18) — which is exactly why managing one well so often means managing the other.
items.cloze: {{c1::5}}. Hypertension and chronic kidney disease exist in a bidirectional, self-reinforcing cycle (Figure 18) — which is exactly why managing one well so often means managing the other.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why do loop diuretics increase calcium excretion while thiazide diuretics decrease it?

options.A: Loop diuretics act in the collecting duct; thiazides act in the proximal tubule
options.B: Loop diuretics collapse the lumen-positive potential that drives paracellular calcium reabsorption; thiazides do not
options.D: There is no mechanistic difference between the two classes

items.why: Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, collapsing the lumen-positive potential that normally drives paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ reabsorption, so calcium excretion rises; thiazides act at the distal tubule and, through a separate mechanism, increase distal calcium reabsorption instead.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient's thiazide diuretic stops controlling blood pressure as CKD advances to an eGFR of 22 mL/min. What is the most appropriate change?
items.why: Thiazide diuretics lose most of their natriuretic efficacy once GFR falls below roughly 30 mL/min. Loop diuretics act upstream at the thick ascending limb and remain effective in advanced CKD.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient starts lisinopril for proteinuric CKD and the serum creatinine rises by 25% within two weeks. What is the most appropriate response?

options.B: Continue therapy with ongoing monitoring, since this rise is expected

items.why: A creatinine rise of up to approximately 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB reflects reduced intraglomerular pressure from efferent arteriolar dilation — an expected hemodynamic effect, not toxicity — so therapy should generally continue with monitoring.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why are ACE inhibitors and ARBs preferred first-line therapy for hypertension in proteinuric CKD?

options.A: They preferentially dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria
options.B: They have no renal effects beyond lowering systemic blood pressure
options.C: They are the only antihypertensive class that can be used in CKD
options.D: They increase aldosterone release to protect sodium balance

items.why: ACE inhibitors and ARBs preferentially dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and reducing proteinuria — a structural renoprotective effect beyond systemic blood pressure control, which is why they are preferred in proteinuric CKD specifically.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic starts a daily OTC NSAID and develops acute kidney injury. What is the mechanism?

options.A: Three independent reductions in glomerular filtration pressure combining additively
options.C: The ACE inhibitor directly damages the NSAID
options.D: This combination has no increased risk

items.why: This is the "triple whammy": the NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole, the ACE inhibitor dilates the efferent arteriole, and the diuretic causes volume depletion — three independent reductions in glomerular filtration pressure that combine additively to synergistically, precipitating AKI.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which drug class is used for BOTH hypertension and angina pectoris via the same underlying mechanism?
items.why: Calcium channel blockers treat hypertension via arteriolar dilation (reducing afterload/systemic vascular resistance) and treat angina via the same arteriolar-dilation mechanism (reducing afterload and myocardial oxygen demand) — the clearest example of one drug class, one mechanism, two indications in this unit.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why does an ACE inhibitor cause a dry cough?

options.B: It blocks AT1 receptors in the lung
options.C: Angiotensin II rises and irritates airways
options.D: Bradykinin accumulates because ACE also degrades it
options.E: It is an IgE-mediated allergy to the drug

items.why: ACE also breaks down bradykinin; blocking it raises bradykinin, causing cough and angioedema (S6).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A woman of reproductive age with proteinuric CKD needs antihypertensive therapy. What must be addressed first with an ACE inhibitor?
items.why: ACE inhibitors (and ARBs) are contraindicated in pregnancy; avoid in women who are or may become pregnant (S5; S7).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why are ACE inhibitors and ARBs preferred in proteinuric CKD beyond lowering blood pressure?

options.A: They raise GFR by expanding volume
options.B: They increase aldosterone to retain sodium
options.E: They are the only class allowed in CKD

items.why: Reducing angiotensin II preferentially dilates the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria (S8; SG U5-R8).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on metoprolol develops heart block after a second drug is added for blood pressure. Which drug most likely?
items.why: Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil) with a beta-blocker risk bradycardia and AV block (S13).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A pregnant patient needs an oral antihypertensive. Which central agent is the preferred option on the slides?
items.why: Methyldopa is used in pregnancy (S12; S16; S50).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why must hydralazine be paired with a beta-blocker and a diuretic?

options.A: To reduce its hepatic first-pass loss
options.C: To avoid hyperkalemia from RAAS blockade
options.D: To block reflex tachycardia and fluid retention
options.E: To prevent rebound hypertension on stopping

items.why: Direct arteriolar dilation triggers reflex tachycardia and fluid retention (S16).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: What happens if clonidine is stopped abruptly?
items.why: Abrupt clonidine withdrawal causes rebound hypertension (S16; S49).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A man using sildenafil asks for a nitroglycerin prescription for chest pain. What is the key concern?
items.why: Concurrent PDE5 inhibitors are an absolute contraindication to nitrates — severe hypotension (S19–S20).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: How do nitrates relieve angina?

options.A: They inhibit PDE5 to raise cAMP
options.B: NO raises cGMP, venodilation cuts preload
options.C: They block β1 receptors to slow the heart
options.E: They block ACE to lower angiotensin II

items.why: Nitrates release NO → guanylate cyclase → cGMP → venodilation, reducing preload and oxygen demand (S19–S20).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why does a patient on long-acting isosorbide mononitrate need a nitrate-free interval?
items.why: Tolerance develops with continuous exposure; a nitrate-free interval (typically overnight) maintains efficacy (S19).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which drug class is used for both hypertension and angina via the same mechanism?
items.why: CCBs dilate arterioles, lowering afterload — treating both hypertension and angina (S22; SG U5-R10).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: What is the most common adverse effect of nitrates, and why?
items.why: Nitrate adverse effects: headache (vasodilation), reflex tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension.

options.A: Yes, if doses are 6 hours apart

items.why: PDE5 inhibitors block cGMP breakdown; with nitrates, life-threatening hypotension — an absolute contraindication.

items.why: ACE inhibitors (-pril) block angiotensin I → II; ARBs block AT1; aliskiren blocks renin; spironolactone blocks aldosterone.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 52-year-old with an intact uterus wants estradiol for hot flashes. What must be added?

options.B: A progestin to protect the endometrium
options.C: Nothing, if the dose is low

items.why: Unopposed estrogen with a uterus raises endometrial cancer risk; add a progestin (S6–S7).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 36-year-old smoker with migraine with aura wants contraception. Which choice fits best?

options.C: A combined pill at the lowest dose

items.why: Estrogen is contraindicated; progestin-only methods avoid estrogen VTE risk and are the correct first choice (S9).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: How do progestins protect the endometrium in combined or hormone therapy?

options.A: They thin cervical mucus to aid clearance
options.C: They block aromatase in the endometrium
options.D: They block estrogen receptors in the uterus

items.why: Progestins bind progesterone receptors, limiting estrogen-driven proliferation and maturing the endometrium (S6–S7).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which adverse effect is specific to depot medroxyprogesterone (DMPA) with prolonged use?
items.why: DMPA specifically causes reversible bone density loss with long-term use (boxed warning) (S6; S9; S31).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 30-year-old with factor V Leiden asks for contraception. Which feature of combined pills drives her main risk?

options.C: Only her age, not the pill

items.why: VTE risk relates to the estrogen, not the progestin, and inherited clotting disorders markedly increase it (p. 772).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why is raloxifene preferred over tamoxifen for osteoporosis prevention in a woman without breast cancer?

options.A: It is neutral at the endometrium
options.B: It does not raise VTE risk
options.E: It antagonizes bone resorption via DHT

items.why: Both are bone agonists; raloxifene is essentially neutral at the endometrium (S11).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 45-year-old premenopausal woman with ER-positive breast cancer asks about letrozole alone. Key point?

options.B: Its main risk is endometrial cancer
options.D: It raises estrogen to fight the tumor

items.why: Before menopause the ovaries are the dominant estrogen source; AIs need ovarian suppression (S13–S14).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: How do finasteride and spironolactone differ in reducing androgen action?

options.B: Spironolactone lowers testosterone production in the testis
options.D: Finasteride blocks DHT synthesis; spironolactone the receptor

items.why: 5-ARIs block testosterone → DHT; spironolactone blocks the androgen receptor (S16).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A man on testosterone therapy has a hematocrit of 55%. What adverse effect is this?
items.why: Testosterone causes erythrocytosis; monitor hematocrit and PSA (S15).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: How does metformin improve hirsutism and ovulation in PCOS?

options.B: Lowers insulin, so ovarian androgens fall
options.E: It suppresses FSH and LH directly

items.why: Metformin reduces hyperinsulinemia’s stimulation of ovarian androgens and raises SHBG — indirect, not hormonal (S22–S23).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In PCOS, how does hyperinsulinemia raise free testosterone?

options.C: It blocks aromatase in the ovary
options.D: More ovarian androgen and less SHBG

items.why: Hyperinsulinemia stimulates theca-cell androgen production and lowers hepatic SHBG (S20).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A woman with PCOS on spironolactone for hirsutism plans pregnancy. What is the key counseling point?

options.B: Continue; it is safe in pregnancy

items.why: Spironolactone: avoid in pregnancy (teratogenic risk; feminization of a male fetus) (S24; S39).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why is metformin called an indirect therapy for hyperandrogenism in PCOS?
items.why: Metformin improves insulin sensitivity and reduces hyperinsulinemia’s stimulation of ovarian androgens — no hormone receptor involved.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 54-year-old with an intact uterus starts estradiol for vasomotor symptoms. What else is required?
items.why: Unopposed estrogen with a uterus drives endometrial proliferation → hyperplasia and cancer; a progestin counters it.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: How do estrogens produce their effects on the endometrium, bone and lipids?
items.why: Estrogens bind intracellular ER-alpha/ER-beta and regulate gene transcription in reproductive, bone, cardiovascular and CNS tissue.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why do finasteride and dutasteride appear in both GU sessions?
items.why: 5-ARIs block testosterone → DHT: hirsutism/alopecia in Session 1, BPH in Session 2.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A postmenopausal woman with osteoporosis and no breast cancer wants a SERM. Which fits?
items.why: Raloxifene is a bone agonist, endometrium-neutral — preferred for osteoporosis prevention without a breast cancer indication.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on the progestin-only pill took today’s dose 4 hours late. What counseling applies?

options.B: Stop the pill for a week
options.C: Switch to a combined pill now

items.why: Norethindrone’s efficacy falls if a dose is more than 3 hours late; taken daily with no pill-free days.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: How do bicalutamide and finasteride differ in reducing androgen action?
items.why: Flutamide/bicalutamide are direct AR blockers (prostate cancer, with a GnRH agonist); finasteride/dutasteride block testosterone → DHT.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Eight months into tamoxifen, a 55-year-old reports new vaginal bleeding. What should happen?

options.C: Add estrogen to stabilize the lining

items.why: Tamoxifen’s endometrial agonism raises hyperplasia/cancer risk — new bleeding needs prompt evaluation.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 38-year-old who smokes daily asks for contraception. Which choice is most appropriate?

options.C: Combined pill at the lowest dose

items.why: Smoking with age over 35 substantially raises estrogen’s thromboembolic risk; progestin-only methods carry no estrogen.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why does tamoxifen raise endometrial cancer risk while raloxifene largely does not?
items.why: SERMs act as agonists in some tissues and antagonists in others; tamoxifen activates the endometrium, raloxifene is essentially neutral.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman with PCOS on metformin is scheduled for a CT with iodinated contrast and has reduced kidney function. Advice?
items.why: Hold metformin for an iodinated contrast study or renal impairment (lactic acidosis).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A man on testosterone injections has a hematocrit of 56%. What is the issue?
items.why: Testosterone causes erythrocytosis; monitor hematocrit and PSA; oral forms risk hepatotoxicity; suppresses fertility.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman on anastrozole asks how to protect her bones. Best advice?
items.why: Aromatase inhibitors cause bone loss and joint pain; bisphosphonates and calcium with vitamin D protect bone.

items.label: Practice-exam question

options.A: Stop the pill for a week
options.E: Switch to a combined pill now

items.why: Norethindrone’s efficacy falls if a dose is more than 3 hours late; taken daily with no pill-free days.

items.label: Practice-exam question

items.why: Flutamide/bicalutamide are direct AR blockers (prostate cancer, with a GnRH agonist); finasteride/dutasteride block testosterone → DHT.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on warfarin starts tamoxifen. What should be anticipated?
items.why: Testosterone and tamoxifen raise INR with warfarin.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman who had a hysterectomy wants estrogen for hot flashes. Does she need a progestin?
items.why: The progestin protects the endometrium; after hysterectomy estrogen alone is acceptable.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman with PCOS on spironolactone for hirsutism plans to conceive. Key counseling?

options.C: Continue; it is safe in pregnancy

items.why: Spironolactone blocks the androgen receptor; avoid in pregnancy (feminization of a male fetus).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which drug interaction blunts tamoxifen’s activation?
items.why: CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine) blunt tamoxifen activation.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman with PCOS and a BMI of 36 has not improved on metformin. Which emerging option fits?
items.why: GLP-1 receptor agonists are increasingly used off-label in PCOS with obesity (weight loss, insulin sensitization).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 54-year-old with an intact uterus starts estradiol for vasomotor symptoms. What else is required?
items.why: Unopposed estrogen with a uterus drives endometrial proliferation → hyperplasia and cancer; a progestin counters it.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: What is the central mechanism linking insulin resistance to hyperandrogenism in PCOS?
items.why: Hyperinsulinemia directly stimulates theca-cell androgen production and lowers hepatic SHBG, raising free testosterone.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A man with metastatic prostate cancer starts leuprolide. Which antiandrogen is often added?
items.why: Flutamide/bicalutamide are pure AR blockers, often combined with a GnRH agonist (tumor-flare prevention).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which adverse effect of estrogen therapy is most tested?
items.why: Estrogen’s VTE risk rises with smoking, age over 35 and VTE history.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why is metformin called an indirect therapy for hyperandrogenism in PCOS?
items.why: Metformin improves insulin sensitivity and reduces hyperinsulinemia’s stimulation of ovarian androgens — no hormone receptor involved.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A postmenopausal woman with osteoporosis and no breast cancer wants a SERM. Which fits?
items.why: Raloxifene is a bone agonist, endometrium-neutral — preferred for osteoporosis prevention without a breast cancer indication.

items.stem: Why do finasteride and dutasteride appear in both GU sessions?

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with migraine with aura wants contraception that also lightens heavy periods. Best fit?
items.why: Migraine with aura rules out estrogen; the LNG IUD is progestin-only and treats heavy menstrual bleeding.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 42-year-old premenopausal woman with ER-positive breast cancer asks about letrozole alone. Best answer?

options.C: It raises estrogen to fight tumor

items.why: Aromatase inhibitors block peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogen; before menopause the ovary dominates (needs ovarian suppression).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 25-year-old with PCOS, irregular cycles and hirsutism (BMI 32) does not want pregnancy. Best plan?
items.why: Contraception for immediate symptom control; metformin for the metabolic driver and long-term diabetes risk.

items.label: Practice-exam question

items.why: Estrogens bind intracellular ER-alpha/ER-beta and regulate gene transcription in reproductive, bone, cardiovascular and CNS tissue.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A man on testosterone gel lives with young children. Key counseling?

options.B: Apply it to the hands only

items.why: Testosterone gels risk secondary exposure; also monitor hematocrit, PSA, lipids.

options.A: Switch rifampin to St. John’s wort

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which receptor and location combination is primarily responsible for keeping the bladder outlet closed during the storage phase?

options.A: Alpha1 receptors at the bladder neck and proximal urethra
options.B: M3 receptors on the detrusor muscle
options.C: Beta3 receptors on the detrusor muscle
options.D: Nicotinic receptors at the detrusor muscle

items.why: Sympathetic norepinephrine acting on alpha1 receptors at the bladder neck and proximal urethra produces smooth muscle contraction, keeping the outlet closed during storage. Beta3 receptors, by contrast, relax the detrusor body (not the outlet) during this same phase.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which overactive bladder medication is generally preferred in an older adult already taking multiple anticholinergic medications?

options.A: Mirabegron, a beta3 agonist with no anticholinergic activity
options.C: Any antimuscarinic agent, since they are interchangeable
options.D: No pharmacologic therapy should be used in older adults

items.why: Because mirabegron works by enhancing beta3-mediated detrusor relaxation rather than blocking muscarinic receptors, it avoids adding to a patient's cumulative anticholinergic burden — a key consideration in older adults, who are more susceptible to anticholinergic-related confusion and cognitive impairment.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why is the combination of a nitrate and a PDE5 inhibitor absolutely contraindicated?

options.A: Both drugs independently raise NO/cGMP signaling, and together can cause life-threatening hypotension
options.B: Nitrates block the PDE5 enzyme, making PDE5 inhibitors ineffective
options.C: The combination has no significant interaction and is commonly prescribed together
options.D: PDE5 inhibitors increase nitrate metabolism, reducing anti-anginal efficacy

items.why: Nitrates raise NO/cGMP systemically (the mechanism behind their anti-anginal effect), while PDE5 inhibitors prevent cGMP breakdown. Combined, these two independent mechanisms produce profound vasodilation and can precipitate severe, potentially fatal hypotension — the same NO-cGMP pathway shown in Figure 16, now viewed as a drug-interaction risk rather than a therapeutic mechanism.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Across this unit, what is the common thread linking alpha1 blockers' orthostatic hypotension risk and the nitrate/PDE5-inhibitor contraindication?

options.A: Both reflect genitourinary drug classes acting on receptor families (adrenergic, NO-cGMP) that are shared with the systemic vasculature
options.B: Both are reasons to avoid all genitourinary pharmacology in older adults
options.C: Both are unrelated adverse effects with no shared mechanism
options.D: Both apply only to patients with no cardiovascular disease

items.why: Alpha1 blockers act on the same receptor family in the bladder neck/prostate and in blood vessels, and PDE5 inhibitors/nitrates both converge on the same NO-cGMP signaling pathway used in both the corpus cavernosum and the vasculature. Recognizing receptor families as the shared variable — not organ system — is what ties genitourinary and cardiovascular pharmacology together across Units 5 and 6.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why is unopposed estrogen avoided in a patient with an intact uterus?

options.A: It significantly increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer
options.B: It has no effect on the endometrium
options.C: It always causes immediate heavy bleeding
options.D: It is only a concern in postmenopausal patients

items.why: Unopposed estrogen drives unchecked endometrial proliferation, significantly raising the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer in a patient with a uterus — this is why a progestin is always paired with estrogen therapy unless the patient has had a hysterectomy.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why does tamoxifen carry an increased risk of endometrial cancer while raloxifene largely does not?

options.A: Tamoxifen acts as an estrogen receptor agonist in the endometrium; raloxifene is essentially neutral there
options.B: Tamoxifen blocks the androgen receptor instead of the estrogen receptor
options.C: Raloxifene has no effect on the estrogen receptor anywhere in the body
options.D: Tamoxifen and raloxifene have identical endometrial effects

items.why: Tamoxifen is a tissue-selective estrogen receptor modulator that acts as an agonist in the endometrium (raising cancer risk) while acting as an antagonist in breast tissue; raloxifene shares the breast antagonist and bone agonist effects but is essentially neutral at the endometrium.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: What is the central pathophysiologic driver linking insulin resistance to hyperandrogenism in PCOS?

options.A: Hyperinsulinemia stimulates ovarian androgen production and lowers hepatic SHBG, raising free testosterone
options.B: Insulin resistance has no mechanistic connection to androgen levels
options.C: Hyperandrogenism always precedes and causes insulin resistance, never the reverse
options.D: Metformin directly blocks the androgen receptor

items.why: Hyperinsulinemia stimulates ovarian theca-cell androgen production directly and lowers hepatic SHBG production, raising free testosterone — the mechanistic link at the center of the PCOS-insulin resistance cycle (Figure 7).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on an antimuscarinic for overactive bladder develops new confusion. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Switch to a beta3 agonist (mirabegron), which lacks anticholinergic activity
options.D: Confusion is unrelated to antimuscarinic therapy

items.why: Mirabegron enhances beta3-mediated detrusor relaxation without blocking muscarinic receptors, avoiding the cumulative anticholinergic burden that can precipitate or worsen confusion in susceptible patients, particularly older adults.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why are alpha1 blockers used for BPH associated with orthostatic hypotension?

options.A: Alpha1 receptors also mediate vascular smooth muscle tone, not just bladder neck tone
options.B: Alpha1 blockers have no effect outside the bladder
options.C: Orthostatic hypotension only occurs with beta3 agonists
options.D: Alpha1 blockers directly block cardiac beta receptors

items.why: Alpha1 receptors are not bladder-specific — the same receptor family mediates vascular smooth muscle tone throughout the body, so alpha1 blockade at the bladder neck also lowers systemic vascular resistance, producing orthostatic hypotension and a first-dose effect.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Why is the combination of a nitrate and a PDE5 inhibitor absolutely contraindicated?

options.A: Both independently raise NO/cGMP signaling, and together can cause life-threatening hypotension
options.B: PDE5 inhibitors inactivate nitrates before they reach the bloodstream
options.C: The combination has no significant interaction
options.D: Nitrates block PDE5 directly, making the combination redundant but safe

items.why: Nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors both raise NO/cGMP signaling through independent mechanisms; combined, the effect on vascular smooth muscle relaxation is additive to synergistic, producing profound and potentially fatal hypotension.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which receptor on the detrusor body relaxes the bladder during filling?
items.why: Norepinephrine at beta3 on the detrusor body causes relaxation during storage (S7).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: During the storage phase, which pattern of autonomic tone is correct?

options.A: Both systems are silent during storage
options.D: Somatic tone opens the external sphincter

items.why: Sympathetic tone keeps the outlet closed (alpha1) and reservoir relaxed (beta3); parasympathetic tone is low (S7; S9).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: How does mirabegron improve overactive bladder?

options.B: Stimulates beta3 to relax the detrusor
options.C: Blocks alpha1 at the bladder neck
options.E: Lowers DHT to shrink the prostate

items.why: Mirabegron enhances beta3-mediated detrusor relaxation without blocking muscarinic receptors (S15; S42).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with uncontrolled hypertension needs OAB therapy. What concern applies to mirabegron?
items.why: Mirabegron can raise blood pressure; monitor in uncontrolled hypertension (S15; S48).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A man with BPH wants fast relief and long-term shrinkage of his prostate. Best plan?
items.why: Alpha1 blockers act in days; 5-ARIs take 3–6 months to modify disease — combine them (S23–S24).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A man on finasteride for 2 years has a PSA of 1.8 ng/mL. How should it be read?
items.why: 5-ARIs lower PSA by roughly half on long-term therapy (S23–S24).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which receptor does the external urethral sphincter use?
items.why: Somatic (pudendal) nicotinic control holds the external sphincter.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why do alpha1 blockers for BPH cause orthostatic hypotension?

options.A: They act only in the bladder

items.why: Alpha1 blockade at the bladder neck also lowers systemic vascular resistance — orthostasis and a first-dose effect.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: During storage, what does norepinephrine do at alpha1 and beta3 receptors?

options.E: Contracts the detrusor and opens the neck

items.why: Alpha1 at the bladder neck contracts (continence); beta3 on the detrusor relaxes (low-pressure filling).

items.why: 5-ARIs can cause ambiguous genitalia in a male fetus; pregnant partners avoid crushed or broken tablets.

items.stem: Which PDE5 inhibitor has the longest half-life, allowing flexible dosing?
items.why: Tadalafil has a longer half-life and more flexible dosing.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 79-year-old with mild cognitive impairment becomes confused weeks after starting oxybutynin. Best change?
items.why: Oxybutynin has the highest CNS anticholinergic burden; mirabegron relaxes the detrusor via beta3 with no anticholinergic activity.

items.why: Nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors both raise NO/cGMP; together, life-threatening hypotension — an absolute contraindication.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on sildenafil starts clarithromycin. What should be anticipated?
items.why: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin) raise PDE5 inhibitor levels.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: What distinguishes tamsulosin from doxazosin?
items.why: Tamsulosin/silodosin are uroselective; doxazosin/terazosin lower BP more; all share orthostatic hypotension and a first-dose effect.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A man on tamsulosin is scheduled for cataract surgery. What should be done?

options.B: Switch to finasteride the day before

items.why: Floppy iris syndrome is a recognized intraoperative complication with alpha1 blockers — preoperative reconciliation.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A man on tamsulosin (no nitrates) wants sildenafil. What is the remaining concern?
items.why: Alpha1 blockade and NO-cGMP potentiation both lower BP — less severe than nitrates but warrants spacing or monitoring.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A man on finasteride lives with his pregnant wife. Key counseling?

options.E: She can crush them for him

items.why: 5-ARIs can cause ambiguous genitalia in a male fetus; pregnant partners avoid crushed or broken tablets.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 79-year-old with mild cognitive impairment becomes confused weeks after starting oxybutynin. Best change?
items.why: Oxybutynin has the highest CNS anticholinergic burden; mirabegron relaxes the detrusor via beta3 with no anticholinergic activity.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.src: L12 S5; S7; S9; SG U6-R11
items.stem: Which receptor–location pair drives voiding?
items.why: Parasympathetic ACh at M3 contracts the detrusor; sympathetic alpha1 closes the neck and beta3 relaxes the detrusor during storage.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why do alpha1 blockers for BPH cause orthostatic hypotension?

options.B: They act only in the bladder

items.why: Alpha1 blockade at the bladder neck also lowers systemic vascular resistance — orthostasis and a first-dose effect.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with poorly controlled hypertension needs OAB therapy. What is the concern with mirabegron?
items.why: Mirabegron can raise blood pressure — monitor in uncontrolled hypertension; it also inhibits CYP2D6.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which pairing of drug and mechanism is correct?
items.why: Mirabegron beta3; oxybutynin M3 (and M2) antagonist; tamsulosin alpha1; finasteride 5-ARI; sildenafil PDE5.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with dementia on donepezil is started on oxybutynin. What is the problem?
items.why: Cholinesterase inhibitors oppose antimuscarinics, and oxybutynin adds CNS anticholinergic burden.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which adverse effect is most associated with sildenafil?
items.why: PDE5 inhibitors cause headache, flushing, dyspepsia and visual disturbance (blue tinge, notably sildenafil).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which adverse-effect cluster follows from antimuscarinic OAB therapy?
items.why: Systemic muscarinic blockade causes dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision and confusion; avoid in narrow-angle glaucoma and retention.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which receptor does the external urethral sphincter use?
items.why: Somatic (pudendal) nicotinic control holds the external sphincter.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A man with BPH wants quick relief and a smaller prostate long term. Best regimen?
items.why: Alpha1 blockers act in days; 5-ARIs shrink the prostate over 3–6 months — frequently combined.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: How do PDE5 inhibitors produce an erection?

options.B: They block alpha1 in the penis

items.why: NANC nerves release NO → cGMP → smooth-muscle relaxation; PDE5 inhibitors prolong cGMP.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A man on dutasteride for 2 years has a PSA of 2.1 ng/mL. How should it be interpreted?
items.why: 5-ARIs lower PSA by roughly half on long-term therapy; adjust when interpreting.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which PDE5 inhibitor has the longest half-life, allowing flexible dosing?
items.why: Tadalafil has a longer half-life and more flexible dosing.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: While counseling a patient, you learn his wife has new vaginal bleeding on tamoxifen. What do you advise?
items.why: Tamoxifen’s endometrial agonism raises hyperplasia/cancer risk; new bleeding warrants prompt evaluation.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with narrow-angle glaucoma needs OAB treatment. Which class is preferred?
items.why: Antimuscarinics can worsen narrow-angle glaucoma and urinary retention; mirabegron has no anticholinergic activity.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: During storage, what does norepinephrine do at alpha1 and beta3 receptors?

options.A: Contracts the detrusor and opens the neck

items.why: Alpha1 at the bladder neck contracts (continence); beta3 on the detrusor relaxes (low-pressure filling).
